subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCES

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply) moved
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 194, to encourage and to assist in the construction of a trans-Canada highway.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments in moving second reading of the bill entitled "An act to encourage and to assist in the construction of a trans-Canada highway".
Hon. members will understand that this legislation is enabling in character, in that it seeks authority for the federal government to enter into agreements with the provincial governments toward the construction of provincial highways which will join at various provincial boundaries to form a continuous road across Canada from one coast to the other and, as such, constitute a trans-Canada highway.
This project has been envisaged for many years, and it is considered that the time is now appropriate to proceed with it. When first contemplated it was conceived as a highway from Halifax to Vancouver, but it is now proposed that it shall extend from Victoria, on Vancouver island, to St. John's, Newfoundland, and also embrace Prince Edward Island.
The highway, when completed, will remain the property of the respective provincial governments, who will assume their normal highway responsibilities with respect to it, such as maintenance and snow removal. In effect, therefore, this legislation will enable the federal government to assist provinces in highway construction.

Nearly all provinces are already heavily engaged in highway programs, and it would be difficult for most of them to assume alone this additional work without some financial assistance. Moreover, the completed highway will have a national aspect in that it will serve to link all provinces, and will enable Canadians to travel from one end of Canada's mainland to the other on Canadian soil by hard-surfaced road. As such, it will play a part in the national economy. Under the circumstances it would appear justifiable for the federal government to contribute up to half the total cost, as the bill indicates.
It is considered, however, that the highway would not be national in scope unless all provinces participated, without which participation the federal government would not be justified in providing this measure of assistance. It was for this reason that we have felt obliged to inform the provinces that the federal government's contribution is being made by reason of the national aspect of the problem, and its participation is contingent upon all provinces entering into agreements with the federal government.
A dominion-provincial conference was held last December, under the chairmanship of the then minister of mines and resources, to discuss this project in a preliminary way; since that time a considerable amount of work has been done by way of working out details and arriving at general agreements with respect to broad principles. Since the project was transferred to the Department of Reconstruction and Supply in March, 1949, officials of the department have visited every province, including Newfoundland, and have had discussions with provincial officials concerned. Subsequently, in August and September, I visited the provinces and discussed policy aspects of the problem with provincial ministers in all provinces but Alberta, where the time at my disposal did not enable me to discuss this problem, but the points have been covered in an exchange of correspondence.
Out of these technical and policy discussions developed certain principles which it was considered might form the basis of ultimate agreements. Moreover, the officials of the department have had discussions with appropriate officials of the public roads administration of the United States, while I, as well as the department officials, have had discussions with the Canadian Construction Association, the Good Roads Association, and other interested organizations, all of whom have been most helpful.
Accordingly, early in September I was able to forward to each provincial government a document containing a number of points which had previously been discussed and

which I hoped might ultimately form the basis for agreements which would enable the project to proceed. Some of the suggested terms of agreement were as follows:
(a)	that the highway should be a modern, first-class, hard-surfaced road, following the shortest practicable east-west route consistent with the needs of the provinces and Canada as a whole;
(b)	that the provincial government would be responsible for the selection of a route in conformity with this definition;
(c)	that except in national parks, the province would arrange for the execution of the work;
(d)	that the highway, when completed, would remain in each province the property and responsibility of the province;
(e)	that the federal government's contribution would be in respect of a two-lane, modern highway;
(f)	that the federal government's contribution would be on the basis of fifty per cent of the cost to the province of completing the highway;
(g)	that an additional contribution would be made on a fifty-fifty basis of the costs to the province for those portions of already existing highway which would be included in the trans-Canada highway;
(h)	that the highway should be completed within a period of seven years;
(i)	that all ordinary maintenance costs during or after the period of construction would be the responsibility of the province;
(j)	that tenders and specifications for contracts would be subject to review by the federal government;
(k)	that inspection of the highway and audit of costs would be the privilege of the federal government.
Suggested standards were also placed before provincial governments, including a width of pavement of 22 or 24 feet, and a minimum right of way of 100 feet. It is recognized, however, that there will of necessity be variations to meet local conditions, and it is emphasized therefore that the various technical specifications were put forward only as suggestions. However, it is our opinion that wherever it is feasible and practicable, the width of the hard-surfaced portion of the road should be 24 feet. Intensive studies have been made, especially in the United States, which confirm what is almost self-evident, and that is that no features of a highway have a greater influence upon the safety and comfort of driving than the width and condition of the surface, especially if the volume of traffic is heavy and moves at a relatively
Trans-Canada Highway high rate of speed. Many authorities hold that to permit the desired clearance for commercial vehicles a 24 foot pavement is required.
However, all provinces have been building paved highways for many years and have developed standards which presumably meet their needs adequately, and no attempt will be made to impose upon them specifications which are unsuitable for their purposes.
Speaking generally, all the foregoing suggestions were well received by the provinces. There are certain points in which various provinces differ, and there are technical details still to be worked out. Moreover, there is the important matter of route. Some of the provinces have already defined their routes, in accordance with the general definition; but others have not, because of an expressed desire not to proceed to that stage until the federal government's legislation is approved. This seemed like a reasonable view, and we have therefore not been pressing for a decision. However, no province has indicated that it does not wish to proceed with its share of the project.
Hon. members will note that the bill incorporates most of the suggestions I have placed before the provinces; but I should like in particular to say a few words more about the financial aspects.
It is estimated that the total cost of the highway of approximately 5,000 miles will be of the order of $300 million, and the bill provides for the payment of the federal government's share up to a maximum of $150 million. This averages approximately $60,000 per mile for new construction as well as highway already built. Where the problem is one of new work, the approach is relatively simple, and the federal government will agree to pay one-half the total cost, on the basis set forth in the bill. Hon. members will see that where highway already constructed will form part of the trans-Canada highway, the federal government is seeking authority to pay to the provinces half the total cost to the province of the construction of that part of the highway. This will have the effect of making the federal government's contribution toward highway remaining to be completed considerably more than fifty per cent.
Let us take, for example, a province where $20 million would be needed to complete the highway, and where that province has already spent $8 million on portions of highway which will be part of the trans-Canada highway route. The federal government contribution to the new construction would be $10 million plus fifty per cent of costs previously incurred,

Trans-Canada Highway or $4 million, for a total contribution of $14 million. If the province applies this contribution of $4 million against the cost of completing the highway, federal money in the $20 million expenditure would amount to $14 million, or 70 per cent. On the other hand, the payment for roads already constructed may be applied elsewhere, as determined by the province, but it is my hope that the provincial governments will use it in such a way that the maximum amount of development and the maximum amount of employment will result.
It is natural to expect that the federal government's assistance to provincial governments with respect to this project will be compared to the federal government's assistance to highways in the United States. I would point out, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that there is no wide difference between the United States formula and that contemplated in the bill before the house. In the United States the federal government appropriates certain moneys for highways, and it is allocated to the various states in accordance with a formula which takes into account population, area, and total mileage; but once the allotment has been determined, it is required that the state match it dollar for dollar. The more money made available to any one state by this formula, the more of its own money that state is obliged to commit. Any unused portion of a state's yearly allocation does not accrue to the state but is returned to the federal treasury if not expended on a dollar for dollar basis during the year.
Some hon. members have a tendency to estimate how much money would have been advanced to the various provinces if the United States type of program had been adopted in Canada years ago. In almost the same breath they say that the provincial governments concerned will not possibly be able to meet the financial commitment required of them by this bill. These two views would appear to be contradictory and to overlook the fact that the provinces would have been obliged to match the federal advances dollar for dollar.
Furthermore, I have heard the criticism that a two-lane 24-foot highway is not adequate and that we should be guided by United States practices in this regard. I would point out that the 24-foot two-lane highway is accepted as adequate for most highways through rural areas, and it is noteworthy that in the United States 95 per cent of the rural highways are of the two-lane 24-foot type.
As I indicated previously, there are still some details to be worked out; but these, too,
[Mr. Winters.!
have been a matter of discussion with provincial governments, many of whom have felt that a number of points should be held in abeyance until the federal government has received legislative authority to proceed. It seemed desirable, therefore, that we should go ahead with the legislation and then invite provincial governments to attend a conference of officials and technicians for the purpose of discussing all matters of technical detail, with a view to resolving all such points to the mutual satisfaction of the provincial and federal governments. As I recall, this point has been put to all provinces, either verbally or in writing, and they have agreed; I therefore propose to proceed accordingly.
When the technical details have been resolved, I propose to ask the provincial governments to sign formal agreements with the federal government so that the project may go forward.
Most provinces have expressed a desire to proceed with the construction of the trans-Canada highway in 1950. I propose, therefore, to move forward with the remaining phases so that all outstanding matters may be resolved and agreements signed in order that provinces will be enabled to proceed with the work in the early spring.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is described as "An act to encourage and to assist in the construction of a trans-Canada highway." Everyone in the house is in favour of the construction of a trans-Canada highway, and no doubt everyone in the house also believes that the dominion government is the only authority that can take the lead in bringing about the construction of such a highway. But in the view of the official opposition this bill is very disappointing. I propose to outline some of the reasons why we are disappointed with the terms of the measure. Perhaps I can best begin to do so by dealing with the situation in the province of British Columbia.
We are remote from Ottawa; we are farther away than any inland province, and for many years we have been tremendously anxious to have a trans-Canada highway. As conditions are at the present time, most of our vehicular traffic goes north and south. If a person in British Columbia goes for a drive he goes down to the state of Washington or to the state of California. A very small percentage of our people drive east to Alberta. If they do drive to Alberta or to eastern Canada, the route followed is almost invariably first of all down to the United States, and then on one of the great United States highways until they are south of the destination, when they drive north into Canada.
For us the United States tourist is of great importance. The states to the south of us are wealthy, and a great many of their people like to drive north; therefore the highways in British Columbia mean a great deal to that province. Because of the mountainous nature of the province we have always been faced with high costs in building roads. The need for help finally became so great that in the early thirties, during the regime of the late Lord Bennett, assistance was given by the federal government for the building of a trans-Canada highway around what is known as the Big Bend of the Columbia river. Help was also given on the roads leading from the United States boundary up into the national parks. I believe the same sort of assistance was given to the province
Trans-Canada Highway of Alberta on the road leading into Waterton national park and through that park up to Banff.
There has been one bad feature about the roads in the national parks, which of course are the responsibility of the dominion government. Restrictions have been placed on the use of these park roads by trucks. I sometimes wonder whether these restrictions are not placed on the roads to help out the railways by preventing freight trucks from going from British Columbia to Alberta over park roads. Whether that is so or not, the fact is that traffic has been impeded by reason of federal regulations in respect to the park roads.
For many years in British Columbia we have believed that there should be a national highways system, not just one trans-Canada road, and that it should include feeder roads from the United States. We realize that such a system could not be completed in a day, but we contend there should be a master plan for a national highways system toward which the dominion and the provinces could be working. That, of course, is what is being done in the United States. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) intimated this morning that his new plan is the same as the United States plan; but I would point out that there is one great difference, namely, that in the United States they have a federal aid highways system- not just one road.
The minister said further that Canada's new road was to be as good as they have in the rural parts of the United States. I do not think that is good enough. I hold in my hand a statement made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in 1948, when he spoke at Kamloops, British Columbia. The quotation is taken from a newspaper dated September 10, 1948. The minister said:
I am going to keep on advocating the building of a great national system of highways which will make it possible for the Canadian people to travel from one end of this country to the other.
On September 11, 1948, at Nelson, British Columbia, the minister told five hundred people that Canada needs a national highway system and that it should be built and maintained by the federal government. He said further: "All Canadians must fight for such a system. You'll get a southern highway a lot faster if you ask to get all-a system of highways-built, than if you ask for one."
It is evident that the Minister of Agriculture has lost out in this decision. But he is not the only one who believes there should be a national system. That is the first reason for our being greatly disappointed by the present measure.

Trans-Canada Highway
Another disappointment is that the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply cannot tell us today where the route is to go. One would think that after all these months and years the government would have some idea as to what the route is to be. We are asked to pass the measure without having that information.
I have read the letters passing between the dominion and seven of the provinces, and from those letters it would appear that as yet there is no decision concerning Nova Scotia. We have not had the papers from Nova Scotia. It would appear that in New Brunswick the provincial government is advocating a route which would go to the city of Saint John, while the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is telling them they cannot have one.

speechtext:
I cannot get the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) to agree with me all the time, but in any event that is my opinion.
To sum up, the bill is disappointing rather than encouraging, and this after a period of waiting of over fourteen years. I suggest that the reason the bill is in these terms is that the government is stalling on this matter of a trans-Canada highway. It is being used as

Trans-Canada Highway a project to provide for employment in hard times. I suggest that that is the reason why we have a bill of this kind. I can see the fine hand of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in nearly every line of this bill. When the minister was asked about the trans-Canada highway last year he made this reply, as reported on page 5497 of Hansard of June 19, 1948. The former member for Portage la Prairie asked the question:

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Is there among the future unemployment relief projects or programs of the government any blueprint for the trans-Canada highway?

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
If we see any sign of widespread
unemployment we will proceed to make a blueprint. But at the present time we have not a blueprint and we do not think one is necessary.
On August 10, 1948, the then minister of mines and resources, Mr. MacKinnon, made a speech about the trans-Canada highway, and a press dispatch of that date is headed: "Trans-Canada highway years away: Mr. MacKinnon." Then there was the Liberal convention, and I understand a resolution concerning the trans-Canada highway was put through. The next step was a conference with the provinces which was called in December, 1948. I have here a dispatch from the Vancouver Sun describing the conclusion of the conference. It reads:
Ottawa, December 16-The dominion-provincial trans-Canada highway conference came to an abrupt and unexpected conclusion Wednesday night with provincial delegates experiencing a frustrated sense of little accomplishment.
And again:
The meetings were closed to the public, and the only official statement following it, from the chairman, Mines and Resources Minister J. A. MacKinnon, talked vaguely of "very satisfactory progress'' and hoped that "a start would be made in 1949" on a national highway system.
This airy optimism was at variance with the statements from provincial representatives, who blamed the federal government for coming into the conference with no proposals or program.
In March the then minister of mines and resources handed over the trans-Canada highway project to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. In the spring session we were told that there was to be a trans-Canada highway bill, but it did not appear on the order paper until more than two months after the house began its sittings, the date being April 8. Nothing was done at that session. Then during this session we heard a significant statement from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) when he delivered his budget speech and said that the magnitude and timing of the trans-Canada highway was to be given very careful consideration, intimating that the government was not in any great hurry about the highway.
The resolution preceding this bill appeared on the order paper two months ago, but was

not called until a week ago, and we are now considering the bill itself in the dying days of the session. This all reminds me of a moving picture of a horse race shown in slow motion. That is how the ministry have been moving with this highway program. They have effectively stalled it over the whole year, although no one in this house or in the country has stated opposition to the measure.
I repeat that all the time the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been in the background; he has had the idea that this should be an unemployment relief project. If the government does not change its tactics in regard to this measure, we may find that development of the trans-Canada highway will be dragged along as slowly as possible.
Even now the government is half-hearted about it and obviously ill prepared. I do not believe the minister has a suitable staff to supervise the construction of this highway; and expert supervision is required. Millions of dollars can be saved by way of specifications if the dominion government has an experienced staff checking on the construction of the highway. Now the departments are to be reorganized, and the next few weeks or months will be spent juggling around the branches, one of which will have to do with this trans-Canada highway. We have an item in the estimates-not in the main or supplementary estimates, but in the further supplementary estimates-for the trans-Canada highway; the only vote I can find. It is item 889, providing $25,000 for preliminary engineering work and studies in co-operation with the provinces concerned. This does not look like speedy action on the highway in the near future. Obviously there is no master plan, no blueprint. The minister does not even know where the road is to go, and no clear-cut policy is being presented to this house, even after all the delay.
The official opposition are disappointed in this measure. We will support it on the basis that half a loaf is better than no bread, but we shall not be content until there is a federal-aid highways system in Canada. This house and the people must not accept the measure which has been brought down today as the final word in the construction of a trans-Canada highways system. We urge that there be no more delay. It is a disgrace that Canadians should have had to wait until 1950 to get action on a trans-Canada highway. Great opportunities have been lost during the fourteen years this government has been in power-opportunities for Canadians to know their country and their countrymen in the other provinces; opportunities for developing Canada; opportunities for extending our means of carrying both goods and passengers.. Just think what would have been the effect

on transportation costs if years ago we had provided a trans-Canada highway-the effect not only on freight rates but also on passenger rates; great opportunities have been lost for expanding our tourist industry; all because this government would not take the lead.
In connection with this project for a trans-Canada highway system, vision is required. The people of Canada have the vision of a national system. What is required is vision here in the House of Commons. I believe we should have before us at all times the vision of Canada as one of the great nations of the world, with a population of fifty, seventy-five or a hundred million people. The bill we are considering today just does not fit in with that vision in any way at all.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the principle of this bill we are in agreement; but coming as I do from Nova Scotia I am not satisfied that any member from that province, with the exception of the minister, can say that he is prepared to have this bill pass in its present terms. I say that because negotiations for a trans-Canada highway have been going on in this country for a long time, and a great deal of work has been done on that highway in Nova Scotia. To what extent it is completed, or what work is still necessary there, we do not know; and until such time as the premier of Nova Scotia is prepared to make available to members of this house the correspondence between his government and the federal government I do not think any hon. member from that province-and there are ten of them on the other side of the house -is in a position to say that the arrangement set out in this bill is satisfactory to the people of Nova Scotia.
Why that correspondence should be considered secret is something I cannot understand. And when the federal government takes the attitude that it cannot make known to this house exactly what are the views of the provinces in this respect, I am led to believe that something is the matter. Why should British Columbia, Manitoba or Nova Scotia take that position? If their proposals are fair and reasonable, or if their objections to the action the federal government is taking have some basis in fact, why should they not be prepared to give that information to members of this house?
This is not a provincial project; whether the premiers of the provinces I have named like it or not, this is a national project. Most of the money will be made available by the federal government before we are finished with this highway, and already a great deal of money has been spent on it by the provinces. That money belonged to the taxpayers,
Trans-Canada Highway not to the premier of our province and his little cabinet. So before I come to a decision on this bill I want any information that may be in the hands of the minister on this matter, and the correspondence that has taken place between this government and the government of Nova Scotia.
I do not understand why the department should take the attitude that it should withhold the correspondence, because, as I pointed out on a previous occasion, there is no law compelling it to do so. There is a law or practice under which that is done with respect to correspondence between this government and a foreign government, but otherwise it is a question of courtesy on the part of the minister. There may be times when it is necessary to withhold correspondence; some premier may write a letter he would be ashamed to have tabled in the house, and under such circumstances perhaps it would be only fair that the minister should withhold it. But this is a straight business proposition; and before I commit the people of Nova Scotia to the payment of fifty per cent of the cost of this trans-Canada highway, 1 want to know what value there is in it. I want to know to what extent Nova Scotia is to be reimbursed for what it has spent already on what will be part of this trans-Canada highway-and a good deal of money has been spent there. Much of the highway construction has been completed in that province; but apparently we are not going to get that information.
The attitude of the government would lead us to believe that correspondence between this government and the provinces has not been tabled previously in this house. This is not so. Many times I have sat in my place here and heard a motion go through for the tabling of correspondence with the provincial governments on many matters. Just at random I picked out one. I wanted to get as close to the maritimes as I could, so I have one which had to do with correspondence with the province of New Brunswick- and on a much more ticklish subject, mind you, than the trans-Canada highway. It will be found at page 4492 of Hansard of June 23, 1947. It is a motion by the member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Hatfield), which reads as follows:
For a copy of a resolution moved by the minister of agriculture in the province of New Brunswick, and all correspondence which passed between the provincial minister and the federal Minister of Agriculture or the Department of Agriculture, regarding a fair price on potatoes under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, 1944.
That motion passed unanimously, and it has to do with prices. If the position had been taken that such a disclosure would

Trans-Canada Highway place the importer or exporter of potatoes in New Brunswick at a disadvantage with his competitors, there would have been some basis for the argument that the correspondence should be withheld. But the motion passed unanimously. Today, when something having to do with the future is brought forward, something which has to do with the spending of public funds in the provinces of Nova Scotia, Manitoba and British Columbia and is vital to the people of those provinces, we are told we cannot see the correspondence.
I am not blaming the minister; he is only a cog in the machine. All he can do is carry out his orders, but I do not think the members of this house should submit to it. I do not believe any member should sit here and say he is going to commit his province to an expenditure of fifty per cent of the cost of this trans-Canada highway, and to the maintenance of that highway, when someone behind the scenes has decided the route by correspondence. The member does not know whether, from a business standpoint, the route is suitable to the province.
I am opposed to this measure until such time as we have an opportunity of seeing the correspondence. I cannot see any reason for holding it back. I might agree with every word the correspondence contained, but I would have to look at it. The government of Nova Scotia is presided over by one man, and he has no right to take the position that the correspondence is not to be tabled. I believe every member from the province of Nova Scotia has a right to see that correspondence. While I approve the principle of the bill, I am going to vote against it until I have heard from the people of Nova Scotia with regard to the project.

speechtext:
This is the first opportunity I have had of speaking on this subject at this session. I have spoken on it on other occasions, but I believe I would be remiss in my duty if I did not say a few words about it today.
Let me say at once that I believe the minister deserves a great deal of credit for bringing the subject of the trans-Canada highway forward at this time. The question is not a new one in Canada; in fact I believe it has been discussed at every session since I came to this house in 1935.
One of the amazing things that I have noticed on my trips to Ottawa is the lack of a national highway. As I have travelled on the Canadian Pacific railway on my journey to Ottawa I have been amazed to see that sections of highway around the head of the lakes are practically completed. When I say practically completed I mean that there are

sections of five, ten, or fifteen miles that are completely graded and gravelled; yet there is no connecting link between those sections.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Oh, yes.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCES
speechtext: The bridges are not even completed.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I have been over it.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
The hon. member must have had some wonderful means of transportation, or perhaps we are talking about different sections of this highway. I am talking about the sections that are built along the C.P.R. track in the province of Ontario, north of the great lakes. It seems to most people in Canada that this national highway would have been built long ago had it not been for the influence that the railways have been able to exert on those in high places. That should not be permitted, and work on the highway should be commenced as quickly as possible. Therefore I wish to congratulate the minister upon his doing the proper thing. The sooner the road is completed, the better pleased the people of Canada will be.
There is no question about it, sir; we need a trans-Canada highway. Possibly I have travelled the road between Ottawa and the west coast oftener than any other member of this house, with the exception of the member for Battle River (Mr. Fair). I have travelled the road between Ottawa and Alberta no less than fourteen times, and sections of it more often than that. I believe I have a knowledge of road conditions. It is extremely embarrassing for a Canadian, Mr. Speaker, who desires to go to Vancouver, Alberta, or Saskatchewan, to have to go through the United States and then back up into Alberta or wherever he is going. It is embarrassing to have the United States authorities say to you: "Well, why did you come this way?" You must tell them that Canada has not a proper road. Then they laugh, and rightly so, to think that a nation as great as Canada cannot afford a national highway. It is a national disgrace, and the minister deserves a great deal of credit for introducing the subject now.
Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that I am of the opinion we should have an all-weather, hardsurfaced highway across Canada. There are not many of the national highways in the United States that are four-lane highways. Most of them are two-lane highways, so I cannot criticize the government too strongly about that at the moment. I say "at the moment" advisedly. It is a good start; but when the government is negotiating with the provinces, provision should be made now for obtaining a right of way which would permit the construction of a four-lane highway. I do not believe it will

oe very long before sufficient traffic will be moving on the all-Canada route, particularly in certain sections of the country, to make it necessary to have a four-lane highway. Once the right of way is obtained, it is exceedingly difficult in many places to get a greater width. It would be more efficient and more businesslike to provide for a right of way sufficiently wide to take care of a four-lane highway, so that when the time arrives there will be no difficulty in widening the highway.
Every province is going to benefit by this highway across Canada. I am sure that the people of Alberta will benefit greatly by an east-west road. There is one road now running north and south across our province, and another road is under construction. Before very long we hope to have two complete highways running north and south. These will act as feeder roads to the main trans-Canada highway going east and west. I believe that is true of every province of Canada.
It will be an asset to the people of every province to have this trans-Canada highway. It will be a great tourist attraction, or at least it should be, to a great many people in the United States. It will be a direct benefit to those in the states directly south of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, because tourists will come up into those provinces and cross over the western provinces on a good all-weather hard-surfaced highway.
The trans-Canada highway should be of great importance in the matter of defence. This factor also should be borne in mind when the highway is being built. It is one of the reasons why a moment ago I suggested that when we are acquiring the right of way we should make provision for a four-lane highway.
If the highway is handled properly, it will be an asset also for trucking. I want to mention that particularly because anyone who has travelled the highways in the United States will have noticed the tremendous amount of trucking that goes on over their national highways. In fact in the United States trucking has become such big business that special roads are being built between large centres such as Detroit and Chicago; these are four-lane highways on which left turns are not allowed; if you wish to turn left you must first make a right turn and then go under a subway. These roads are called express highways and are used for the swift movement of motor vehicles of all kinds, including the automobiles of tourists, but particularly the heavy trucks.
Trans-Canada Highway
We must bear in mind the fact that this road of necessity will be used for trucks and trucking. The government would show exceedingly good judgment if they left this road free for trucking and did not bring it under the control of the board of transport commissioners. One of the reasons why the United States has made such great progress is that free enterprise has been allowed to operate. It is true that if trucking is permitted it is going to affect the railways a great deal, but the railways will have to modernize themselves to cope with the competition which is bound to come.
My mind goes back to the time when we enacted legislation in this house giving the railways an advantage over trucking in the agreed charges; that legislation put trucks at a great disadvantage. Now we are to have a national highway, and if we are to hamstring the trucking business and make it conform with all the desires of the railways, it seems to me that we shall retard the progress of this country rather than advance it.
I was interested in reading an article which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of Wednesday, November 23, 1949. It is headed: "Present brief in behalf of truckers." Speaking about the competition of trucks and railways, it had this to say:
The trucking industry yesterday told the royal commission on transportation there is "discrimination against highway transport in Canada."
Opening its submission before the three-man body investigating national transportation problems, the Canadian Automobile Transportation Association entered these complaints:
1.	Commercial truckers are barred from the haulage of feed grains from lake ports to inland points on which the federal government pays a subsidy to farmers under a feed-grains assistance policy.
2.	A ban on through hauls by way of national parks against commercial motor vehicles is "intended to protect the railways."
3.	Commercial motor vehicles are not given fair treatment on the Canadian National Railways ferry linking Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. A previous complaint to this effect had been made by the island government.
4.	Trucks are barred from carrying most forms of alcoholic liquor from the United States into Canada.
John Magee of Toronto, executive secretary, delivered the brief for the C.A.T.A., which represents federations in six provinces with a membership of 5,000 trucking firms.
Five thousand trucking firms is no small business; when you consider the amount of haulage that is done by these trucks, you will see that it is exceedingly large business. The proposed trans-Canada highway is to traverse national parks. If the federal government in the future takes the same attitude that it has taken in the past with regard to trucks passing through national parks, then of course they hamstring the trucking business. Trucking on the national highway will just be negligible, because obviously trucks cannot go from one province

Trans-Canada Highway 10 another on the trans-Canada highway if they are not permitted to travel through national parks. The present attitude of the government is that they will not permit this haulage to go through national parks. The railways therefore have a decided advantage over trucking. This situation leaves them in a position to dictate charges. We have the same thing now under the agreed charges, where the railway can go to a large company and say: We will haul your freight, provided that we haul it the year round. To large companies such as Eaton's which bring a great deal of freight from the east to the west and have to go north of the great lakes in the wintertime, the railways say: If you do not give us your business all the year, we will not haul it for you in the wintertime.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCES
speechtext: They cannot do that.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
They do it; make no mistake about that. Under the agreed charges, they do it. That is one of the reasons why our transportation system has been so bad. If we make the condition the same on this national highway, it will be a bad thing for Canada. I think that particular business should be left entirely free and competitive. The railways will just have to modernize their facilities in order to meet the change in times.
Let me say a word about the construction of the national highway. The undertaking that the minister has gone ahead with is no easy thing; it is no simple matter to construct a highway that will stand up. The minister is proposing, at the outset I hope, to build a two-lane highway; that is a good start. I hope he will take into consideration the suggestion I have made of providing for a four-lane highway when the right of way is acquired.
The minister expects there will be about 5,000 miles of highway-and I would assume that judgment is sound-with a total cost of about $300 million, the dominion's share being about $150 million, the federal government to assume fifty per cent of that cost. I am of the opinion that some provinces-and at the moment I am not speaking about Alberta-will not be able to take advantage of this proposal if they have to put up fifty per cent of the cost. We in Alberta of late have been fortunate in obtaining additional revenues through the expansion of the production of oil. But it must be remembered that oil is a depleting asset, and those in charge of the business affairs of that province are well aware of that. Some of the other provinces are not in so fortunate a position. If these other provinces find themselves unable to take advantage of the fifty

per cent to be paid by the federal government, and cannot complete their section of the highway, it just means that the highway will be ineffective, because no one is going to travel from here westward to Winnipeg on a hard-surfaced road and then not be able to go any farther owing to the fact that that province was not able to build its hardsurfaced highway. They will go from here to the United States thence to the Canadian west, and leave in that country the money they would otherwise spend in Canada.
The minister estimates that about sixty per cent of the 5,000 miles is already hardsurfaced. He may be correct on that but I am a little sceptical. I think the sixty per cent is a little too high. From here east most of the highway would be hard-surfaced. Whether it is in sufficiently good condition to be used as a trans-Canada highway I am not in a position to say; but certainly from Ottawa west nothing like sixty per cent is hard-surfaced.
The minister spoke of a hard-surfaced top of 24 feet. That would probably be about the average of the hard-surfaced tops of United States highways. But there is one provision I have not seen in the bill, Mr. Speaker, which I think should be considered. When a hard-surfaced highway is built, for safety reasons if for nothing else there should be a four-foot gravel surface on each side of the hard surface so that trucks or cars, if they have a flat tire or have to pull off the road for any other reason, may be able to do so, in safety. This is one of the greatest criticisms I have of hard-surfaced roads, particularly in western Canada. I speak now of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. On nearly all of these highways there is no place by the side of the road to which you can go to make necessary repairs. It is a very serious thing. It would be safe to say that on these hardsurfaced roads at least fifty per cent of the fatal accidents are caused by cars parking on the hard surface. In the regulations that the government are submitting to the provinces they should of necessity make provision for a four-foot gravel section on each side of the highway. I see the minister nodding his head. I presume it will be included in the regulations, and it is a worth-while thing.
Let me come to another aspect of this question, namely, the maintenance cost. The federal government is not undertaking any obligation at all for maintenance. When the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) spoke on this question he referred to the fact that in Alberta we are saddled with a provincial debt which was created by

borrowing money to build roads and highways. Many of the roads which were built thirty or forty years ago are completely gone, but we are still paying for them. Since the Social Credit government came into power in Alberta every foot of highway that has been built in that province has been paid for. I do not care how good a road you build, it is going to deteriorate. The minister says that this program is to last for seven years. I venture to say that if this national highway was started tomorrow, by the time it was completed, at the end of seven years, sections of it would have to be rebuilt, depending on the type of soil that you must travel through. This is a major consideration in building a highway. I see the minister shaking his head the other way now. Nevertheless it is a fact that in some sections of the country, depending upon the soil texture, the road will deteriorate faster than in others. I do not care what kind of trans-Canada highway you build, in at least twenty years some major repair work will have to be done on it. The provinces will not be in a position financially to take care of that maintenance in addition to paying fifty per cent of the actual cost of construction.
In all fairness it seems to me that the federal government should assume at least a portion of the maintenance cost, having in mind the fact that within seven to fifteen or twenty years sections of the road will have to be rebuilt. I have never seen a highway yet -and I have travelled over a great number of them-either in Canada or in the United States, parts of which had not to be rebuilt from time to time. I know of one important highway in the United States, forty or fifty miles of which were built four years ago, and last year they were tearing up the whole surface and rebuilding it. They had probably run into some very poor soil, and that section of the road was not standing up as well as other parts of it. What will be the position of the provinces in circumstances such as these? That kind of repair may well be classed as maintenance or upkeep. Neither the maritime provinces nor the western provinces will be in a position financially to carry out these heavy maintenance charges in certain sections.
I do not think I should say a great deal at this time as to the route of the trans-Canada highway. I know that many suggestions have been made to the minister as to where the road should go. It seems to me that when you are building a road like this the governments and people of the provinces should be just about as good judges of the route as anyone can be. Consideration will have to be given to many problems. Certainly one of the 45781-1494
Trans-Canada Highway important advantages of a national highway will be its attraction of tourists. When tourists come to a country to spend their holidays they want to see something. Among the most worth-while attractions in Alberta are Banff and Calgary, of course, as well as Lake Louise and the icefields. These are attractions which cannot be duplicated anywhere else in the world, and if you have no highway there, you are going to lose business. When I say the route should be left to the good judgment of those in charge of the provinces, I mean just this: that the Alberta people are going to feel that the route must go through Calgary, for the very obvious reasons I have indicated. In leaving a certain amount of latitude in this regard to the provinces, the minister has shown exceedingly good judgment.

speechtext: So long as the highway goes through Calgary.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate because I would not like the idea to get abroad that those of us from Vancouver or from British Columbia think that this is a disappointing bill. I hope that the spirit pervades in that meeting which I think should pervade in the House of Commons, namely, that a British Columbian should be just as much interested in the efficiency of the trans-Canada highway as it affects the constituency of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis)

Trans-Canada Highway as in its efficiency in British Columbia. This should be the spirit, because it we are to have a trans-Canada highway we want to have a highway on which we from British Columbia can travel right through to Nova Scotia and the other provinces, and on which they can travel to our province.
One of the greatest advantages will be that of bringing together the people of the various provinces. I believe the figures I shall place on Hansard will be of interest to hon. members from all the provinces, because they show the cost of road construction where we have to gouge out mountainsides, and where the roads hug the hills, with precipitate clearances into rivers from heights sometimes as much as 800 or 900 feet.
We have done an enormous amount of road-building in British Columbia in recent years, and are proud of it. We are particularly proud of the 24-foot Hope-Princeton highway. I am sure if the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra were to go over it with me he would agree that it is ample for British Columbia, and will be for many years to come. I drove over it recently from Keremeos to Penticton in forty-five minutes; not many years ago it would have taken an entire day to make the trip.
Here are some of the figures-and I would ask hon. members to keep in mind the fact that they show the cost per mile, exclusive

of hard-surfacing. This is just for the road building, up to the point where it can be hard-surfaced. The cost per mile of the Ashcroft-Cache Creek road was $30,806; the cost of the Chase Village road was $81,689 per mile for a small piece. For the Westbank-Trepanier highway the cost was $50,289 per mile; for only four-tenths of a mile on the Boston Bar road-and how lucky we were that it- was only four-tenths of a mile-the cost was $99,000, or at a rate of $247,500 per mile. This was clear blasting of rock; and I would draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that it is part of the trans-Canada highway. The Chum Creek-Squilax highway cost $54,545 per mile. The trans-Canada highway at Robbins Creek cost $166,250 per mile-and all this to draw up the road, without hard-surfacing. We have spent on section A of the Hope-Princeton highway $2,773,127.85, or $104,646 per mile. That was for a distance of 26-5 miles. Section B of the Hope-Princeton highway, for a distance of 56-5 miles, cost $3,371,496.81, or $59,672.50 per mile.

Trans-Canada Highway position in which the hon. member endeavoured to place me a short time ago when he said that I had seduced the Minister of Agriculture-that is the term he used-aw^y from Amherst, Cumberland county, to Halifax. There is one respect in which I differ with what the minister said in his statement. If we are to undertake the building of a national highway we should start with that in mind. I suggest that instead of a 22- to 24-foot two-lane highway, provision should be made for a four-lane highway-perhaps not right through the whole distance, but certainly fn those parts of the country where there is likely to be fairly heavy traffic.
In California and other parts of the United States they started with two, three and four-lane highways, but subsequently they were forced to widen them to six and eight-lane highways. That widening was done at great cost because of the increased value of the property which had to be taken over. We should realize that the first cost is the cheapest, and provide for a four-lane highway where traffic warrants such a width.
I am not going to deal with the tourist question, except to say that I am entirely in accord with the resolution and the bill. I feel that this money will be more than an expenditure; it will be an investment. The results will be shown by the attitude of those who visit this country. Just last evening I heard General Wavell speak over the radio in high terms of the progress made in Canada. speechtext:
When the house rose at one o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I had been referring to the fact that I was in accord with the general principles of the legislation introduced by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters). I recall that in 1936 the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who I believe was then Minister of Transport, brought in a transport bill

Trans-Canada Highway which not only dealt with rail and air travel but also gave the provinces an opportunity to share jurisdiction over the highways. At that time the provinces, quite rightly, took exception to the provisions of part 3 of the bill, which dealt with highways. They felt that highways came strictly within the jurisdiction of the provinces and that for this reason they should not be dealt with by the bill. Subsequently that part of the bill was dropped, and the legislation dealt only with transportation by rail and air, and a portion of water transportation.
I believe the same views are held by the provinces today, except that they are willing to co-operate in a much greater degree. I do not wonder that they have assumed that position, because the proposition that has been placed before them is very generous. Almost any businessman would be prepared to enlarge his business if he had to put up only fifty per cent of the cost; and that is practically what the government is offering the provinces under the terms of this legislation. As a matter of fact they are doing better than that; they are saying, "We will match your contribution dollar for dollar to the extent of $150 million. Then when the work is finished, in seven years, the entire proposition will be yours. You may collect the licence fees, take advantage of the tourist traffic, and derive all the other benefits that may accrue from a national highway." So, notwithstanding what was said by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), who did not see how the Nova Scotia members could vote for this bill, as far as I am concerned I look upon this as a splendid opportunity not only for Nova Scotia but for all the provinces.
In bis statement the minister said he did not see how he could go ahead with this project unless all the provinces agreed. I say to him and to the government that they would be quite justified in carrying out the agreement with as few as five provinces, if only that many signified their willingness to take advantage of the legislation. I believe the minister would be well advised to proceed in such case, without waiting for the rest of the provinces to come in. I offer that as a suggestion because the proposition looks so good to me. I really cannot see why any province would hesitate to come under the legislation which was so clearly explained by the minister this morning.
As the minister stated, this is simply legislation of an enabling nature, to permit the provinces to take advantage of the offer if they feel so inclined. It would be wonderful, I think, for Canadians living in the

extreme west or in the central provinces who wanted to visit Nova Scotia, that beautiful ocean playground on the extreme east, to be able to travel the entire distance over a Canadian national highway. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) suggested that the road be extended southward to the United States, but I do not agree. We are very pleased to receive tourists from the New England states and particularly to have our native sons who are now living in Boston and the surrounding district pay us visits, but I think our first duty is to provide a national highway which will serve our own provinces.
Returning to the question of the advantages accruing from this highway, as far as the provinces other than Quebec and Ontario are concerned, it seems to me that from a business point of view those other provinces would be well advised to enter into this agreement, because of the great possibility in connection with tourist trade. According to the census of 1941 Quebec at that time had a population of 3,331,882 and Ontario 3,787,655. I think we all appreciate what this means to the other provinces as far as the tourist business is concerned. During the past few years we in Nova Scotia have been very fortunate, in that we have had tourists from every state in the United States. I also noticed them from British Columbia, Saskatchewan and other provinces of Canada. The great majority of western tourists who come to the maritime provinces, however, find it necessary to travel by the southern route, through the United States. It is unfortunate that this should be so, but I am sure that situation will be remedied after this legislation goes through this house and is endorsed, as I am sure it will be, by all the provinces of Canada.
I do not say this in a political way at all, and I would not want the hon. member for Cumberland to think I was doing so; but there has been a wonderful improvement in the tourist traffic in Nova Scotia in the last fifteen years. People have come from all parts of Canada and, as I mentioned a moment ago, from all over the United States to enjoy the wonderful scenery we have to offer in our province; and they all leave speaking in the very highest terms not only of the hospitality they have enjoyed but of our fine highways. I believe great credit is due the premier of Nova Scotia, Angus L. Macdonald, for the progress that has been made in this regard; and again I do not say this in any political sense at all.
In his remarks this morning the minister said this program would cover a period of some seven years. I sincerely hope it will not take that long. I fully appreciate that the

construction of five thousand miles of paved or hard-surfaced road is a big undertaking, but we all recall what was done in connection with the Alaska highway. There we have a road sixteen hundred miles long, twenty-four to twenty-six feet wide, extending from Dawson Creek in British Columbia to Whitehorse and Fairbanks, Alaska. In the spring of 1942 that was virgin territory, the only means of transportation a pioneer air route. In November, 1942, it was officially opened for military traffic. So I say the minister may be able to shorten the period of construction, so that instead of seven years we may look forward to seeing this project completed in perhaps four to five years. If that can be done the various parts of Canada will enjoy that much more prosperity from the tourist traffic.
I said I was going to be brief in my remarks, Mr. Speaker. I certainly did not wish to let this opportunity pass, however, without adding my voice to those who have so warmly welcomed the legislation that has been placed before us by the minister. He stated his case clearly, and there was no misunderstanding what the government was prepared to do. I simply wish to accord him my full support.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words with reference to the matter which is before the house. I believe the proposal to construct a trans-Canada highway has received the approval of all members from all sections of Canada. As has been stated by the previous speakers, it is not a new idea. The matter was considered by the provinces and then the war intervened, otherwise I have no doubt that the trans-Canada highway would have been built by now.
I feel that it is a splendid idea to link the provinces of Canada together. The more the people of the various provinces visit one another, the stronger Canada will be. There has not been enough of that in the past. In the province of New Brunswick, we are in a rather peculiar position. Upon looking at the map one can see that this province is the link between the provinces of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and the rest of Canada. Because of this, I feel there are problems facing the province of New Brunswick which are not found in the other parts of Canada. I do not envy the position in which the minister finds himself in attempting to work out the details, because I am sure there will be a great divergence of opinion in the different provinces as to the route of the trans-Canada highway.
During the last election campaign in my own province, as I remember, three different
Trans-Canada Highway routes were mentioned by the local government. I might say that all three of them went through my constituency, so I was impartial. Just to indicate the difference of opinion as to the route this highway should follow through the province of New Brunswick, I should like to read some of the correspondence in that connection which took place in November of 1948. The deputy minister of public works in the province of New Brunswick, Mr. Barbour-who I might say is one of the most efficient public officials in Canada-replied to a letter from Mr. Wardle of the Department of Mines and Resources. It is dated November 25, 1948, and reads in part as follows:
It is the intention of the government here to set out the trans-Canada highway as follows:
No. 2 from the Quebec border north of Edmunds-ton down to Fredericton; thence across the Saint John river and following No. 9 along the shore of Grand lake to Sussex: and thence to the Nova Scotia border near Amherst and to Cape Tormen-tine for connection to the island.
Evidently that was the decision of the New Brunswick government in November, 1948.
There have been some changes since then, and on January 24, 1949, the Minister of Public Works, the Hon. W. S. Anderson, wrote to the Hon. James A. MacKinnon as follows:
It has now been found advisable to change the route-
Speaking of the route of the trans-Canada highway.
-and we suggest No. 2 highway from the Quebec border to Fredericton with a branch into Saint John through Oromocto following route 2A to Westfield and thence into Saint John. Also for the benefit of Nova Scotia and island traffic the trans-Canada highway would cross the Saint John river at Fredericton following route 9 to Sussex and thence through to the Nova Scotia border and connect with the island at Cape Tormentine. This has the effect of lengthening the trans-Canada highway by 21 miles.
I am sure that must be a mistake. It can be seen from that letter, however, that there was a change and the government felt that there should be two routes from Fredericton; one down through Oromocto, and then what is known as the broad route through Westfield and into Saint John. From Saint John it would follow No. 2 to Moncton. It was also suggested that for Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia traffic, in order to shorten the distance in travelling to those provinces, the highway should follow No. 9 from Fredericton to Sussex and then into Moncton.
The next letter referring to this subject is dated September 29, 1949, written by Hon. W. S. Anderson to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters). It reads as follows:
As explained before the trans-Canada highway passed through Saint John to Moncton-

Trans-Canada Highway
He means the route that was laid out when the trans-Canada highway was mentioned some years ago.
-and thence to the Nova Scotia border, but in order to make a shorter route we did suggest No. 9 highway from Fredericton to Sussex in order to cut off distance.
That rather indicates that the government was willing to drop the second proposed route from Fredericton over No. 9 to Sussex, and accept the route from Saint John to Moncton.
On November 4, 1949, the provincial minister of public works wrote to the Hon. Mr. Winters. He was replying to a letter in which the minister of reconstruction set out the general program for the trans-Canada highway. Speaking of the general concept the provincial minister said:
It is submitted that this should be amended to read "the most practical route across Canada and each of the provinces." For reasons set out in my letter to you of September 29 we cannot reconcile ourselves to any route through New Brunswick which will by-pass Saint John.
That became the definite policy of the government. On September 19, the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply wrote Hon. Mr. Anderson stating:
The choice of the route of the trans-Canada highway across each province rests with the province.
That is quite a definite statement.
The federal government is of the opinion that it should1 follow the shortest practical east-west route across each province, consistent with the needs of the province; and that the trans-Canada highway as a whole should follow the shortest practical east-west route across Canada consistent with the needs of Canada as a whole. The federal government's participation in the cost would have to be conditioned upon those factors being given adequate consideration.
On this basis, and as indicated in my discussion with the Hon. Mr. McNair, the federal government would consider appropriate modification from your original submission of January 24 last regarding the location of the highway in New Brunswick. The route on which it is believed that the federal government should contribute (completion costs and back costs) is as follows: Entering New Brunswick from a point on the Quebec boundary north of Edmundston and following highway No. 2 to Fredericton, thence to Sussex over highway No. 9, from Sussex to Aulac through Moncton over highway No. 2, and from Aulac to Cape Tormentine over highway No. 16.
The minister does not definitely state he will not accept the proposition made by the New Brunswick government but he strongly suggests that the route which the dominion government is prepared to accept is the route I have just described.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, I feel that the minister is going to have considerable difficulty in persuading the different provinces that the shortest east-west route is the one which they must accept. I might also point

out that, so far as the province of New Brunswick is concerned, its portion of the trans-Canada highway will carry the cars, trucks and so on from Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and the traffic from the United States which goes through New Brunswick into Quebec, Ontario and the west. The cost of maintenance of the highway in the province of New Brunswick is going to be a heavy one; I think it will certainly be much heavier than in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island and undoubtedly it will be much heavier than in the province of Newfoundland.
The minister used one expression, "the needs of the province", which I think needs some explanation. When the minister speaks again I think he should explain to the house just what he means by "the needs of the province". From reading the correspondence here, it is rather hard to know just what is meant by that expression. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) spoke about the great tourist traffic. One of the needs of our province is more tourist trade. If we are to have a trans-Canada highway for that particular need, it should be built in that section of the province which will induce the most tourist traffic. Another thing that might be considered a need is the shortest route between the larger centres of population. If that is a need, that would have to be taken into consideration. I am sure that the general term "needs of the province" has little meaning at all.
As to the cost, I would also point out to the minister that, like some of the hon. members who have already spoken, I feel that the cost is going to be a heavy burden on the smaller provinces, particularly on our province of New Brunswick. I think we shall have more mileage per capita of population than any other province in Canada. The trans-Canada highway will traverse the whole length of the province of New Brunswick, north and south. This morning the minister said, I think, that the total mileage would be about 5,000. It is estimated that the mileage in New Brunswick will be about 450. I do not know how much it costs to build a mile of hard-surfaced road in Canada today, but I think the average for my province is around $100,000 a mile.

The minister shakes his head. I do not think my estimate is far out. Having regard to the high cost of material and the high cost of labour, I would not be at all surprised if he finds that this trans-Canada highway, 5,000 miles in length, cannot be

built for the $300 million which he has mentioned. I am satisfied that in New Brunswick alone it will cost from $25 million to $30 million.
I should like to point out this fact. We in the province of New Brunswick today are the heaviest taxed province in the Dominion of Canada. We have the highest per capita debt. We pay more for our gasoline than do those in any other province. We also pay more for our car licences. If an extra burden like this is added to those already carried by the people, without more assistance from the government, I think it will be exceedingly difficult for a small province like New Brunswick to bear the expense. I think we in New Brunswick have more road mileage, including hard-surfaced and gravel roads, than any other province in the dominion.
I have here in my hand the Canada Year Book, 1948-49; at page 709 there is a statement of construction, maintenance and general expenditures on rural highways, bridges and ferries in Canada by provinces, 1942-46. I am sorry that I could not get the figures for 1948 and 1949, but I think 1946 is a fair year. The construction expenditures in the province of New Brunswick in 1946 amounted to $7,032,089. I will compare that figure with that in the province of Manitoba, in which it was only $2,143,505. Everyone knows that Manitoba is a much richer province than New Brunswick. We all know that the population of Manitoba is perhaps double that of our own province. Yet their cost for highways was just about one-third of what it was in our province. The cost in Saskatchewan in that year was $4,372,502, a little over half as large as ours. In Alberta it was $6,205,275. In British Columbia, a province with many times the wealth of ours, and a population of over twice what it is in New Brunswick, the construction expenditures were $5,887,779 or just slightly more than half what we spent in New Brunswick. I will not give the figures for the larger provinces, but in proportion they work out at about the same ratio.
Then I come to the maintenance expenditures. For the maintenance of our highways in New Brunswick in 1946 we spent $4,144,259; Manitoba spent $1,189,168; Saskatchewan, $1,784,940; and British Columbia, $2,931,839. By comparison, one can see the burden that the construction, maintenance and upkeep of roads is in a small province like ours.
Then, as to administration and general expenditures, in New Brunswick in 1946 the figure was $573,806; in Manitoba, it was $311,227; in Saskatchewan, $165,187; in Alberta, $22,461 and in British Columbia it was $686,319, slightly more than in New 45781-150
Trans-Canada Highway Brunswick. I am simply quoting these figures, Mr. Speaker, to indicate to you that the burden which will be placed on New Brunswick is going to be a serious and heavy one.
I think the question of constructing highways comes into the picture. In New Brunswick it is difficult to construct highways. We have many rivers, brooks, streams, hills and other impediments that are not found, for instance, in Saskatchewan or many parts of Alberta or Manitoba. It is going to cost far more per mile to construct the trans-Canada highway in our province than it is in any of these other provinces. In equity, I think that such a province as New Brunswick should receive in compensation from the federal treasury more than the fifty per cent which the minister mentioned this morning.
Another point which I should like to call to the attention of the minister is the width of the road. I think perhaps his statement was such as to indicate that some changes could be made. He said it would be 100 feet. Most of the roads constructed in the maritime provinces are 66 feet wide. Along the border of the road there are rows of trees that have been there from 50 to 100 years. There are buildings right up to the edge of the road. If the minister insists that the road be 100 feet wide, I can see much difficulty in widening the roads through the maritime provinces. These are old localities. The difficulty will be very great.
Another matter which the minister should take into consideration is the question of railway crossings. I do not know how the construction of the road will be carried on in other parts of Canada, but the part that is suggested along the Saint John river from Edmundston to Fredericton has many level crossings. A highway of this kind, which is being built to encourage traffic from one end of the country to 'the other, should be a safe one. On a public highway of this kind everything should be done to provide for the safety of the people using it. When the minister brings in his final bill I hope that some provision will be made to ensure the safety of railway crossings.
There is another point which should be taken into consideration. I do not know whether this is a problem in other provinces as it is in ours, but when work is provided on our highways the practice has grown up of giving that work almost entirely to government supporters.
