speechtext:
I shall not delay the house very long. First of all I wish to congratulate the minister on this bill, No. 194, to assist in the construction of a trans-Canada highway. I congratulate him on being the first cabinet minister in 1949 to recognize what just about everybody else in Canada has recognized for the last fifteen or twenty years, namely, that the building of the trans-Canada highway is a matter of national importance, and a project for which the federal government should take some responsibility.
I think this is one bill on which we can all agree, at least on the principles of it, regardless of our provinces and regardless of our political differences. This is a matter of great concern to the country, and it is one that I am sure people from all parts of Canada and of all political parties in Canada will appreciate.
There are some things about the bill that I like, and there are some things that I dislike. I am not going to emphasize the things that I dislike because I feel that this bill marks the first step taken by the federal government in the building of a trans-Canada highway. From the minister's remarks I presume he believes that the government can put $150 million into this project over a period of seven years and then pull out of the project entirely. Quite seriously, Mr. Speaker, I doubt whether the minister believes that. I doubt whether he believes for one minute that the federal government can enter upon this project, stay with it for a few years, and then turn it back to the provinces. Let us examine the idea that once the road is built the federal government 
wiU bear no part of the cost of upkeep. I am quite sure that once the minister sits down with the representatives of the provinces, once they get down to the serious business of the details of this project, he will find that the federal government, having gone into the building of the highway, will not be able to get out. I recall that many years ago the government took much the same attitude on a grant for agricultural education and technical education. It was to be a grant for a few years, and then the matter turned back to the provinces. Experience showed that once the government had gone into that business it just could not get out. I am quite confident that as time goes on we shall find the present minister, or some other minister, coming back to parliament year after year with amendments to this legislation which will indicate that the federal government is bearing an increasing proportion of the cost of upkeep of the highway.
I welcome this legislation because it is a step in the right direction, and I look upon it as merely a first step, and not by any means one that is finished in this bill.
There are a few points I should like to raise on which the minister can probably give us some more information. I am not quite clear as to how this $150 million is to be allocated to the provinces. In a general way the minister indicated that it would be allocated on the basis of population and on the cost per mile of highway. I am sure the house would welcome a clearer statement, if it is possible for the minister to give it. The house would like to know just what general formula will be adopted in the allocation of the $150 million. I wonder whether the minister can tell us if this $150 million, if it is matched by the provinces, thus making $300 million, will give us five thousand miles of good hard-surfaced highway as he expects. I hope that part of that $150 million is to be used to reimburse the provinces on a fifty-fifty basis for moneys they have already spent on provincial highways that will form a part of the national highway. Has the minister any estimate as to how much of that $150 million will be used to reimburse the provinces for work that has already been done? In other words, can we arrive at any conclusion as to just how much of this $150 million is likely to be spent on the construction of new highways?
He has told us that the question of routes to be followed will be left to the provinces, and, as other speakers have said, in that I agree with him. I cannot blame the federal minister for not wanting to tackle the particular problem of deciding, for instance, whether the highway is to go through the Ottawa valley, or whether it is to go up to

Toronto, and then up Yonge street to North Bay. I can quite understand why the minister would prefer to have the provincial authorities settle that problem.
That is only with reference to Ontario. There are other sections of the highway where there will be just as great differences of opinion as to the choice of routes. I am confident the government will have to face in time-and I feel certain the government of necessity will do it in the future-the building of not just one trans-Canada highway following any definite route. There are a number of places all across the country where alternate routes are needed, and where two or more alternate routes have advantages.
I certainly visualize the time when, having spent the $150 million of federal money on the building of one highway-and I am not particular which route that highway follows -we shall then follow that up by building alternate routes. For instance, in Ontario such alternate route might follow the Ottawa valley, or go around by Toronto, Yonge street and North Bay. In northern Ontario it might go through Kapuskasing, with an alternate route following the Canadian Pacific along the north shore of lake Superior. A similar situation has developed in the west.
I believe that in future this condition will have to be met, and not by one highway. The minister and other members of the cabinet might as well make up their minds now- because they will have to do so later-that they are not going to get off by contributing to just one trans-Canada highway following one definite route. There will be considerable national advantage in having alternate routes in certain provinces, and possibly feeder lines from certain points on the United States border so as to make it convenient for American visitors coming to this country to reach the trans-Canada highway. Those feeder lines will be just as important a part of the trans-Canada highway as the main highway itself.
If the minister thinks for one moment that the federal government is going to get away with building only one route, contributing $150 million over a period of seven years, and then pulling out of the project and leaving it to the provinces, he is not taking a realistic view of the situation. Indeed I doubt whether that is the point of view held by the minister.
There has been some comment concerning the authority the act will give to the minister. One section for instance states that the minister's authority will include supervision over the calling of tenders, and gives him the authority to review specifications. I would express the hope that the minister's intervention in this sphere may help to some extent 45781-150j
Trans-Canada Highway to curtail the degree to which patronage enters into the building of our highways. It is possible that the power given the minister under the act could be used for that purpose. On the other hand it could be used to increase the use of patronage in the building of the highway, in which event we would have involved not only provincial but federal patronage.
Any hon. member who has any knowledge of what has happened in connection with the building of highways will realize at once that there is no one phase of public works that has been more bedevilled by political patronage than the building of our highways. If the minister's help and influence can be used to prevent the injection of political patronage, or to eliminate it even in some small degree, and if he will make a serious and honest attempt to obtain good value for the dollars spent in highway construction, I am sure the country will benefit.
If the minister can give us a little more information as to the formula to be followed in the allocation of funds to the provinces, and an estimate of how much of this $150 million is likely to go back to the provinces as reimbursement for money they have already spent, and how much will be available for new construction, it will be helpful. He might feel free also to give us his own view as to whether he honestly believes the federal government should go into this business for seven years, spend $150 million and then turn the whole thing back to the provinces.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with some diffidence that I rise at this time to speak as briefly as possible. However, this is the first time I have spoken in this session.
Before proceeding further may I compliment most sincerely the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters). Speaking in the name of my constituents let me say, "You are doing a wonderful job, young man. You are following in the footsteps of your predecessor and have shown yourself enlightened and progressive in all your activities."
I was somewhat puzzled this morning when I heard my good friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) insinuating that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) might have had some ulterior motives in presenting the trans-Canada bill. If I may speak for myself and for the people I represent, I would say that in the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) we have one of the finest statesmen this country has ever produced. He did a marvellous job under difficult circumstances during wartime. He has accomplished things that have evoked

Trans-Canada Highway the admiration of the whole civilized world. He has been a great help in placing Canada, industrially, financially and commercially, in her present high position.
Why it has been found necessary in a discussion of this kind to impute certain motives to that worthy gentleman is beyond my comprehension. So far as I am concerned, and so far as northern Ontario is concerned, I believe I speak unanimously for all in that part of the country when I say that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is a man among millions who has accomplished things worthy of this country and of the whole civilized world.
Just one word about the fifty per cent contribution. There is no doubt that perhaps next year or within two or three years this legislation will be subject to some changes and amendment and the matter will be up again before this House of Commons for discussion. It is not fixed absolutely because, in dealing with this, time and cost factors are involved that must necessarily be reconsidered. I remember when the Quebec-Chi-coutimi road was constructed it was expected that this would cost the province of Quebec $6 million, but up to date it has cost over $20 million and it is not yet completed. We cannot fix an absolutely definite figure for a matter of this kind for the reason that there is so much involved in it. The sum of $150 million is mentioned but it is possible that with the high cost of labour and materials that figure will be increased before the trans-Canada highway is completed.
I should like to say a few words about the routing of the trans-Canada highway. Happily for our people our constituency is in central Canada, geographically speaking, and we are always ready to take a national view of things. We appreciate the problems of the three western provinces in the routing of this trans-Canada highway, and we understand something of the difficulties faced by British Columbia in routing this highway through the Rocky mountains. I know the situation in Ontario and I know something about the problems faced by Quebec and, to some extent, those of the maritime provinces including Newfoundland.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) belongs to a party that is very sensitive about so-called provincial autonomy and provincial rights, but he wants this government to overlap the activities and prerogatives of the provincial governments in connection with highways, a matter which under our constitution comes absolutely within the jurisdiction of the provinces. I wonder what would have been the reaction of the official opposition and its members

if the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) when presenting his bill this morning had said that this government had decided on the route of the trans-Canada highway. I would like to have heard what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) would have said if we had attempted to take away provincial rights in that connection. The Liberal party takes a back seat to no other party in upholding provincial rights and maintaining the integrity of the provinces, and it will not change its position on this question.
A project of this kind should be considered as a national project. The trans-Canada highway should be national in scope. If you study the history of our country for the last forty years you cannot help realizing that great advances have been made in the northern sections of Canada, in northern Quebec, northern Ontario, the northern sections of the three prairie provinces and in northern British Columbia. In dear old Quebec during the last thirty years they have accomplished wonders in colonizing and settling the northern sections of that country. At the present time there are half a million of new population in the northern sections of Quebec. Those people are prosperous and comfortable. They have a really balanced economy because there is good land in the clay belt and the mineral resources have only been scratched up to the present time. There is great potential in hydro power and forest production.
The same can be said of northern Ontario, and we know what is taking place at the present time in Labrador. We have only to read the reports of the geologists to realize the great potentials in power and mineral production that are there. The same thing applies to northern Manitoba, northern Saskatchewan, northern Alberta and perhaps to a greater degree to northern British Columbia. If I were not considering this matter from a national point of view I would say that the trans-Canada highway should be routed northward from North Bay to Hearst to Geraldton and so on. But I am not going to argue that that route should be followed because I believe that the statesmanship of the leaders of Ontario is such that a really national route will be decided upon, and that the claims of the section just mentioned cannot be set aside.
When we are discussing the routing of the trans-Canada highway we must think in terms other than those having to do with the tourist business. The tourist business is important, but this is a national matter. Probably we shall not be building another trans-Canada highway for fifty years or more.

The ten provinces and the central government will have to get together and exercise their intelligence so that a truly trans-Canada highway in the full sense of the word can be provided for the Canadian people.
It will not be possible for all the large centres of population to be on this highway.
I believe the people of Toronto and many other cities appreciate that situation. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) has said that all these large centres will be connected directly or indirectly with the trans-Canada highway. We should not have parochial or local feelings about this matter. We do not want to set up a cabal that will cloud the issue. We must remember that the trans-Canada highway will serve a great purpose in national defence.
We all hope and pray that war will never come, but we remember what happened during the last war. I remember the central government and the government of Ontario got together in order to build a section of highway from Hearst to Geraldton, and Fort William. This was done for national defence purposes. I repeat that not only will this trans-Canada highway serve national and international purposes; it will serve national defence purposes as well. Let us be logical in dealing with this question. I hope that in dealing with this matter the government of Ontario will have a national and not a parochial approach. I know this is a hard question for the provincial administrations to settle. I know that some people in my section of the country will not be satisfied unless the road goes through there because our claims have logic behind them, but after all I think they will be ready to accept loyally any route that is decided upon that will best serve Canada as a whole. That is the only way that a problem of this nature should be discussed.
One word about the maintenance of the road. We speak in general terms of our national economy and we want lower taxation as far as the federal treasury is concerned. Everyone wants to see expenditures cut down. This total of $150 million is a lot of money. It is not the government's money; it is the money of the Canadian people. Before the trans-Canada highway is completed no doubt the federal treasury will be called upon to pay an extra $50 million or $100 million.
I repeat that I believe in the maintenance of provincial autonomy and therefore I believe that highways should continue to remain under the jurisdiction of the provinces. Otherwise we shall have a duplication of services. Ontario has already constructed large sections of highway that no doubt will
Trans-Canada Highway become part of the trans-Canada highway and this applies also to other provinces. At the present time the province is maintaining those roads which in many instances are hard-surfaced. The province has the necessary equipment and personnel for winter and summer maintenance. We would not like the federal government to take over any of those activities as there would be overlapping; as far as I am concerned I would strongly oppose anything like that. I want the prerogatives of the provincial government to be maintained in their entirety. But I go further on that score. If after a year or two, or longer, any province or all the provinces find the maintenance load is becoming too great for them to carry, I think it should be in order for them to come to the federal government with their pleas and arguments, and I am sure they would be received with an open mind.
I repeat that as a national parliament we have a responsibility to the people whom we represent to see that the money of the federal treasury is spent through the proper channels. I make that statement deliberately, because while many times we are told how expenditures may be curtailed, at the same time we hear suggestions for even greater expenditures. When a bill of this kind comes along, for instance, even if it proposed to expend three times the amount mentioned here some people would be asking for twice as much again. During the war I was Deputy Speaker and chairman of committees, and at one time I began to keep track of how much the opposition wanted the government to increase its expenditures; but after I reached a total of $5 billion I stopped.
That is the sort of thing we must guard against at all times because, I repeat, there is no mystery as far as governmental expenditures are concerned. The money comes from only one source; that is, the Canadian taxpayer. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), whose remarks are always very interesting, wants this bill enlarged right away. He says the government has been too slow in bringing forward legislation dealing with the construction of a trans-Canada highway, but in practically the same breath he wants the federal treasury to stand the cost of constructing transverse lines running north and south to the United States. Let us complete one big project at a time; then other problems can be considered. But let me repeat that we must have due regard for provincial rights and provincial autonomy in regard to certain matters which are the primary responsibility of the provincial government and highway administration is certainly one of them.

Trans-Canada Highway
There may be complications with respect to roads already built. That would apply more particularly to the older provinces such as Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Certainly it would apply to Quebec, because you can travel the length and breadth of that province on fine highways. More than that, a few years ago, if I am not mistaken, under Mr. Bouchard, who was then a minister in the Quebec legislature, the construction was commenced of that fine highway called Bouchard boulevard. Now what use is to be made of that boulevard? As far as I can make out it will depend upon the provinces of Quebec and Ontario coming to an agreement. This just illustrates the difficulties that may arise, which can be solved only if the members of all the provincial legislatures work together in a spirit of co-operation.
Then instances may arise where the cost will be either greater or less than in other cases, because you cannot follow rigid lines when working on a project of this kind. There will be many complexities to be met and overcome. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said the government was slow. Well, I don't know. It seems to me this legislation is well timed. Is this not the logical time for it, a few years after the war? Surely no one will contradict me when I say it would have been impossible to start this work during the war. There was a period of six or seven years when it was absolutely impossible to even mention the construction of a trans-Canada highway. At the moment, though there may be local instances of unemployment only a few months ago we actually had over-employment, if I may call it that. The cost of material has been exceedingly high, and as I said a few moments ago we must be extremely careful. We may be budgeting for a trans-Canada highway that we think will cost $300 million, but by the time it is completed the cost may be $500 million.
These are some of the precautions the government must take. The legislation speaks in terms of a period of seven years. Well, I hope it will be completed in less time than that, but there are bound to be obstacles and delays; situations may arise which we cannot foresee at the present time, so that seven years may not be long enough. For a nation acceleration may not be always a good quality. It is true that we must work as quickly and as diligently as possible, but in a matter of this kind we must employ logic and thorough study at all times. Who can say that this fine project may not be completed in five years. Certainly the fact that the legislation mentions seven years is no reason to criticize it.
[Mr. Bradette.l
As to the route to be followed, I know that not a single premier, provincial minister or official of any of the ten provinces will criticize the central administration for not itself deciding upon the route. I am sure all the premiers and their legislatures are prepared to accept their responsibilities as they come along. This morning the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra mentioned that New Brunswick had not definitely decided what route the trans-Canada highway should follow in that province, and there was some question about whether it should go through Saint John. That is one instance showing the difficulties the provinces must expect to face. Once this becomes a fait accompli, however, once the route has been decided upon, I am sure the Canadian people have enough common sense to accept the decision, if not gladly, at least loyally, and in that respect I am sure I can speak for my own section of the country.
When I hear of the proposed expenditure of $300 million for the construction of a trans-Canada highway I am pleased I know that it is a necessary project; I am proud of my country, because we need that national artery which will provide a wonderful means of more closely uniting our ten provinces. At the same time I must think in terms of the colonists, the settlers and farmers of northern Ontario, whom I know so well. Some of them have spent forty years in colonizing that part of our country, and they still have to go through quagmires of mud all summer, and are faced with impossible roads all winter. I like to see cars going along our highways at fifty, sixty or seventy miles an hour, with the people singing and happy. At the same time, having been a colonist and settler myself in northern Ontario, when I am in my own car travelling on our good highways I always have in mind those thousands of settlers and farmers in northern Ontario and also other parts of Canada who, with their wives and children, have to plow through mud and deep ruts all summer. If it had been possible I should like to have seen this legislation include provision for the expenditure of perhaps $25 million for rural roads on a fifty-fifty basis with the provinces. That is just a wish I am expressing, not with any desire to throw cold water on this fine scheme but so that people may realize that this is still a pioneer country and will be such for many years to come, because in northern Ontario, yes in the whole of northern Canada, we have the richest heritage on earth, which so far has just been scratched. The Pre-Cambrian shield offers us the greatest riches any country could wish to possess; that is why I am making these statements at this time.

I am absolutely in favour of the construction of the trans-Canada highway as rapidly as possible; but while that construction is going on I shall always have in mind the many farmers in all our provinces who are suffering through lack of proper roads. I do not say that in a critical way at all, but just in order that this national forum may realize that a section of our population which has done so much for the development of Canada in the last forty years, particularly northern Canada, should receive some consideration from the federal treasury in the near future.
Patronage has been mentioned; and I hope this can be avoided. I know whereof I speak, because in my youth my father, who was engaged in road work, was fired because he happened to be a Liberal. I would not want this to happen to anyone, because it is not Canadianism; it is not worthy of our nation. So I hope there will be safeguards to ensure that no one will be fired, no one will be hired, and no one will be refused a contract because he happens to belong to a party other than that which is in power at the time. Those are the things I know, because no one has been able to accuse this administration of patronage for the last sixteen years, and this is as it should be.
There is one clause with which I entirely agree, and I believe it will be of great help in building this highway. It is the clause in connection with tenders, which states that tenders and specifications shall be reviewed by the minister. I understand that in the province of Quebec there are no standards set for highway construction and no tenders for road contracts. I am not saying this critically, but the federal treasury must insist upon all necessary safeguards in all the provinces so far as contracts are concerned. I repeat that I hope there will be no patronage in the letting of contracts for construction, or in the hiring of workers so far as this great undertaking is concerned. It is necessary to take all safeguards. The Canadian people must be seized of the fact that this is a national undertaking in the full sense of the word, and that it will take the genius and ability of the people of the country to see that it is carried to a successful conclusion.
I believe that is all I want to say at the moment. Before resuming my seat I wish to express the hope that the provincial governments and the central government do not permit themselves to be swayed by the various factions, so that they will avoid having our trans-Canada highway look like that comic strip, the Toonerville Trolley, as it would if it went into all these little corners. We want a highway that will be as straight
Trans-Canada Highway as possible from coast to coast, one which will exemplify the fine spirit of the Canadian people, and which will show that it is possible for all parties in Canada to get together to give to the present and future generations a link that would mean so much to their comfort, happiness and prosperity, and better understanding.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure and a privilege to follow the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. He has one of the most interesting personalities among members I have met during my time in this house. I have always believed in the principle of confederation which I have often said is akin to the principle in the old Cornish battlecry, "Each for all and all for each". I believe that is a good principle on which to base any solution of these grave problems that confront the people of this country after two long wars.
I rise to support, in a general way, the principle of this national project. As a social and economic necessity, it outranks anything of which I am aware, but it is subject to the reservation I always make, that it must be commensurate with the ability of the country to pay. Consideration must be had for the fact that we have taken part in two long wars, and that there are many national problems coming up each day. At the time of Sir Charles Tupper this country was spending $36 million per year, but it is now spending almost that amount in a day. The capacity of the country to pay has to be considered.
I wish to give the government some constructive suggestions in connection with this problem. Some of these suggestions were made by the leader of the opposition, and one concerned the capacity of the provinces to pay the amount named in the bill, fifty per cent of the cost. The leader of the opposition has stated he believes the determination of this percentage should await a provincial conference, and that is correct. Until such time as the various provinces know what revenues they will receive, it would be impossible for them to decide on this economic question.
I wish to deal with some of the economic problems involved in this problem, first from the local standpoint, and second from the national standpoint. Back in 1911 when Sir Robert Borden came into power, he appointed a former provincial cabinet minister, Frank Cochrane, who was then representing a new Ontario constituency, just as my friend does who preceded me in this debate, as minister of railways and canals. Mr. Cochrane had been the Ontario minister of lands and forests. He decided that Toronto's contribution to

Trans-Canada Highway good roads could be reassessed against the proposed federal road from Montreal to Windsor.
I wish to refer to the problem from a local standpoint. As you know, the city of Toronto was a pioneer in the building of good roads. The other day I referred to the fact that milk and dairy products could not be brought into the city-the children had no milk-because of the bad roads. I proposed a resolution, and we conferred with ihe county of York and the province of Ontario about it. I urged the city to give a voluntary contribution to improve the highways around our city from the east, the north and west. This embraced all the surrounding communities, including the riding of South York, which a member of the C.C.F. party represents at the moment. The city went into this scheme and, with the county of York, paid the cost of building good roads for fifteen miles around the city.
I am glad to see that the minister has included in the bill one principle which was not contained in the resolution so far as I could see, that provincial governments would be given credit in this national project for any work done towards making good national roads. Now, that takes me back to the Beveridge bill, which was introduced by the United States government. What was the Beveridge bill? I think the principle of it has been copied into this bill. The minister knows a great deal about this problem. I have found him to be a very industrious minister, and one who looks ahead. I believe this Beveridge bill was passed in 1916 or 1917, and the whole of the national project was paid for with federal funds. But it compelled the various states-what we call provinces-to have a standard contract with Washington on a national standard plan. The federal government paid up to fifty per cent. As long as they had standard plans for the highway they could qualify under what is known as the Beveridge national highway bill. It was one of the finest national bills that I think the United States ever had. They were pioneers in the good roads movement. I think that has been explained in connection with the new provision which the minister has in the bill. It makes it a national work.
I remember when the city of Toronto proposed going in on the Hamilton highway, when Mr. Cochrane was the minister of railways and canals. A deputation of us came down to Ottawa; I think the members were from Hamilton, Toronto, Oakville and other places. We met the government to discuss the matter. What was done was this. The city of Toronto went in by agreement with the city of Hamilton and the Ontario government. To do what? To build the Hamilton

highway. We were to pay only forty per cent of the capital cost of the work. That did not include upkeep or maintenance. In the contract I insisted on having a term specifying a direct route from A to B. Afterwards the Ontario government appointed what was known as the Ontario-Hamilton highway commission, a provincial government commission. What did they do? They just tacked something on to the agreement and made it retroactive. They compelled the city of Toronto to pay forty per cent of the costs for the total upkeep of the work, which accordingly exceeded by a large sum the capital sum; and it was not to go from A to B direct. It was to make a detour past certain people's farms at a place whose name I just cannot think of now. It went up the lake-shore road, and thence down into the village of Oakville. It was then a village; it is now a town. It went thence along past certain people's farms and it was not a direct route at all. The result was that it added greatly to the cost of the work. In the second place, it was retroactive and it compelled the city, notwithstanding the honourable agreement we had with Hamilton and the Ontario government, to pay forty per cent of the upkeep costs. That should not have been.
Then a deputation from Toronto, Hamilton and other places came down to Ottawa about the matter-the Borden government had come into power in 1911

and waited on the then minister, Frank Cochrane. The minister said this national road was to be part of the Windsor to Montreal national highway, and that Toronto would be recouped its share of the costs, including capital and maintenance. I am glad to see that in the amended bill there is some provision made for it now.
I may say that the public wants to see the correct picture in connection with this national highway. As a municipal officer I found that our city, which was the pioneer on the local end of it and many other national features, was not objecting, although it is the main tax-paying city of the dominion. As far as I can see, we do not wish to offer any opposition provided we are able, which we are now under the new amendment, to get contributions in respect of highways previously constructed. There should be some way of working out that plan in the national picture accordingly.
I shall speak for only three or four minutes more. I am sorry that in the early twenties the national railways, which recently had been taken over by the Meighen administration and united into a national system now known as the Canadian National Railways, and the Canadian Pacific railway were not a

little bit more progressive than they were after the first war. I remember in 1920, 1921 and 1922 when we were urging them to go into the motor bus and motor truck systems, they backed up on it and said they had no funds for it. They could not see what the good roads movement meant to these railways. They might have got the cream of the business. Instead of that, they have turned it over largely to private ownership, to the trucks and buses. I was sorry that in any solution of this problem the national railways lost track of that particular matter. The railways were not progressive enough to take advantage of the situation, with the result that they themselves created the situation by which they are done out of the cream of the truck and bus business when they could have had it just for the asking. It would have acted as a feeder to the same railways and would have kept them from going bankrupt and applying for increases in rates as they are doing in various sections of this country at the present time. It would have provided a large revenue for these systems. I am sorry they did not go into it.
As to the annexation of these various districts to which the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) referred, we found that it was far better, instead of annexing these various outside sections of the city- and many of them are in the city now-to give them certain municipal services like water, sewers, good roads, health regulations, police protection, fire protection and the general municipal services. We found that it was better to do that than to annex them, bring them into the city and give them many of the other services which would have been given at the expense of the taxpayers as a whole.
I doubt if there is any city on the North American continent that has contributed more to the good roads movement than our city of Toronto. There is no bigotry in that city. There is a warm feeling for the people of the east and of the west, as was shown last Saturday. I believe that what I say today many others will take up tomorrow. I was speaking to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), through you, sir, the other day about the expansion of the cabinet. I said he would have a cabinet of sixty, and he told me I would not be one of them. I never wanted to be one of them. I point to that consideration. I told him it looked more as though we would have in the cabinet a committee of one hundred; it might go to that. It is the same with other problems. What I say today, probably others will say tomorrow. But that does not make any difference. Our city is one which has been built up by
Trans-Canada Highway progressive people. Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few remarks on this bill.
Trans-Canada Highway First of all, I should like to thank the government for this legislation which is so generous to the provinces. I also desire to compliment the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) on the clearness of the explanations he has given us in connection with this measure. I am aware that, as a trained civil engineer, he is particularly fitted to assume the responsibility of such a project.
If my information is correct and also if what I have read from time to time is consistent with the facts, all provinces or a majority of them would accept the generous bill introduced by the federal government. The stand taken by most members who have made some observations this morning and this afternoon shows that it is admitted in principle that this bill is in the best interests not only of the country at large but also of each province.
I think it would be quite unnecessary to dwell at length on the touristic, economic and military advantages offered by this bill. That is why I was astonished this morning by the statements of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). He brought forward so many objections that, although he finally agreed with the principle of the bill, one could have inferred he was against the measure as presently proposed. Actually the hon. member would have the federal government pay one hundred per cent of the construction costs and also pay costs of maintenance.
Well, under the circumstances, it would be easy to infer that in letting the federal government pay one hundred per cent of construction costs, and later pay for maintenance, it would be a recognition of the federal government's jurisdiction over this highway. Although I am neither a lawyer nor an expert on constitutional issues, I think we all agree that the question of provincial roads, legally speaking, belongs exclusively to the provinces, even if provincial roads have to be used in part for the trans-Canada highway.
Mr. Speaker, I now ask the house again, hasn't the Liberal party always shown that it aims to protect provincial autonomy, that it will not change its attitude as one hon. member, apparently expressing the opinion of the Progressive Conservative party, did this morning? We have always maintained the same policy in respect of provincial autonomy. The minister, in his talks with the provincial premiers or the provincial ministers of highways, has always been careful not to encroach

Trans-Canada Highway upon provincial autonomy. This bill, as all members will agree, is another striking example of the eagerness of the Liberal party, which has been attacked on various occasions, to maintain and protect provincial autonomy.
I hope that the press, especially that of the province of Quebec, will spread the news that once again the Liberal party is giving tangible proof of its absolute respect for provincial autonomy.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra was critical about another aspect of the measure. He asserted that the seven-year period was too long for the construction of that highway. I do not claim to be an expert in the matter, although as a civil engineer I have had some experience in road-building. However in the opinion of specialists, contractors would be unable, with their present set-up and equipment, to build this road in less than ten or twelve years. That period could possibly be reduced to six or seven years, if the provincial authorities preferred to secure the services of contractors from other provinces. As everyone knows, every province-and especially Quebec-keeps a jealous watch over its autonomy. I believe it would be very difficult to use contractors from outside to do the work. That is my answer to the point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. The seven-year period is entirely logical, but time alone will tell more conclusively whether it should be extended since we lack the physical means to complete the work in such a short time.
In this respect, I believe that, without in any way dictating to provincial authorities, it is quite proper for a member of this house to stress, in the course of such a debate, the interests of his constituency. Hon. members, and more particularly the Quebec representatives, know that in 1940 or 1941 that province started to build a highway on the south shore between Quebec city and Montreal. This boulevard, named after Sir Wilfrid Laurier, has many good points. For instance it is 160 feet wide, which incidentally makes it well in keeping with the provisions of the bill now before the house. It could therefore serve as a splendid extension of the trans-Canada highway.
May I suggest to the hon. minister that in his future discussions with the ministers of the provincial departments of highways, he should point out to the minister of highways of the province of Quebec the advantage of selecting this splendid road begun in 1940 or

1941, but discontinued later on. National interests would be well served if this section were to become part of the trans-Canada highway, since it would be completed sooner and at less cost. In addition, it would reduce the distance between Montreal and Quebec by fifty per cent.
This route would provide many advantages to the city of Montreal and the surrounding district. However, we feel it would provide even greater advantages to the Quebec, Gaspe, North Shore, Charlevoix, Lake St. John and Chicoutimi districts.
I do not wish to labour the point, but I hope the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply will put forward all the arguments in favour of this route, in which my hon. colleagues from Lotbiniere (Mr. Lapointe), Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Boisvert), Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Cloutier) and Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cournoyer), as well as those from that part of the south shore of the St. Lawrence are greatly interested.
I am not doing this for political reasons, but it does seem to me that this is an excellent occasion to show all the advantages of this route. I therefore consider it to be my duty to explain these advantages to the house.
Mr. Speaker, those are the few remarks which I wanted to make. I would have liked to address the house in English, but, unfortunately, I only had a few minutes during the noon recess to prepare these remarks.
Such a bill well demonstrates that the Liberal party is not furthering its particular ends in this matter, and that the construction of this highway is intended to foster the economic development of all the provinces. We are showing once more our desire to work in the interests of the nation as a whole. I hope that the highway ministers of the other provinces will approach this matter in a spirit similar to ours for the good of the country as a whole.

Mr. Speaker, in common with the other members who have taken part in this debate, I wish to congratulate the minister on his presentation of this bill. I do hope that a trans-Canada highway will be built as a result of this move. I should like to point out, however, that the position of the government today is quite different from the position it took at the

dominion-provincial conference on highways last December. In this connection I have previously pointed out that the western provinces understood the federal government would be prepared to pay one hundred per cent of the cost of construction of the highway.
I was sorry to hear the minister state that the provision calling for every province to agree to pay fifty per cent of the cost before work could be undertaken in any province would still apply. I noticed that the minister said he felt sure most of the provinces would start construction work in 1950. I am sorry he could not give the house assurance that all provinces would commence construction in 1950. In my opinion the $150 million provided by the bill will be found inadequate. I question, too, the wisdom of paying the provinces for part of the cost of the work they have done on the trans-Canada highway since 1930. I should like the minister to give us the figures to show what each province has spent on its portion of the trans-Canada highway from 1930 to date. It seems to me that such a provision might result in an unfair distribution of a large part of the $150 million. It would seem to me that it might be an encouragement to some of the provinces to do little work on the trans-Canada highway. If a province knew it had $10 million or $20 million coming to it for work undertaken since 1930, then it might use that money for other services or in other ways than building roads.
I should like to deal, Mr. Speaker, in particular with one statement the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply made in introducing this measure. He said that the pattern followed by the government in relation to the trans-Canada highway was similar to the pattern followed in the United States, and that the federal government would pay fifty per cent of the cost of construction. I wish to point out that the formula and policy followed by this government in respect to the trans-Canada highway is much different from the highway program being followed by the United States government. I need only mention that this government does not propose to pay one dollar to the provinces to aid in the construction of secondary or farm-to-market roads.
The government does not propose to pay fifty per cent of the total cost of taking the trans-Canada through some of our large urban areas. Certainly, the program and pattern followed by the government of Canada with regard to highways is far different from the program followed in the United States. Another example of the difference in attitude is that the introduction of a bill
Trans-Canada Highway which will provide some money for the construction of a trans-Canada highway comes thirty-seven years later than the initial highway program undertaken by the United States in 1912.
The United States has a good highway system, as all hon. members are aware. According to the public roads administration annual report for 1948, the United States has a primary highway system totalling 231,977 miles. If Canada had a primary federal highway system which would give us the same number of miles of road per capita as exists in the United States, we would have 20,878 miles. The most that the trans-Canada highway will represent is approximately 5,000 miles.
The next great difference between the program of this government and the program in the United States is that in the United States the government has already contributed towards the construction of a secondary federal highway system composed of farm-to-market roads, school bus roads and rural mail delivery routes. The secondary system in the United States totals 377,622 miles of road. If this government made a contribution to the provinces of Canada to give the same number of miles per capita in a secondary federal highway system as the United States has, we should need to have a system composed of 33,986 miles of road. The total highway system in the United States as of June 30, 1948, towards which the federal government paid a portion of the construction costs, amounted to 609,599 miles. If the Canadian government did exactly the same thing as the United States government, on the basis of our population the federal government should contribute to a highway system composed of 54,864 miles of road. The 5,000 miles of road in the trans-Canada highway will amount to only one-eleventh of a highway system that is necessary to give Canada the same number of road miles per capita of population. If we compare that trans-Canada highway seven years from now, and if we assume that it is built and completed, then the federal government seven years from now will have aided in the construction of a total number of road miles equalling only eight-tenths of one per cent of the total highway system in the United States to which the United States government has contributed.
Another way that the proposed legislation varies greatly from the legislation in the United States is that no consideration is given to the increased cost of taking the trans-Canada highway through our large cities. I might quote a sentence from the

Provision of federal-aid funds specifically for urban improvements and the emphasis that has been placed on the construction of expressways as the only solution of the traffic problems for larger cities have led many cities to substitute bold and direct methods for ineffectual procedures that did not produce results.

In New Mexico, the total cost of all road construction in 1948 was $12,623,954; the federal contribution was $8,045,461. In that year the federal government paid to the state of New Mexico 64 per cent of the cost of the construction of all roads in that state.
In the state of Wyoming in the same year the total cost of all roads was $9,178,227; the federal contribution, $5,972,801. As its share of the cost of construction of all roads in the state of Wyoming for that year the federal government paid 65 per cent.
In the state of Arizona, in the same year, the total cost of all road construction was $8,823,178; the federal contribution was $5,824,907. In that year the federal government paid 66 per cent of the cost of all road construction in the state of Arizona.
The last state I wish to mention is Utah. In that year the total cost of primary road construction was $4,151,691 of which the federal government paid $3,038,871. The total cost of secondary highways was $2,733,167, of which the federal government paid $2,032,511. In the state of Utah for that year the total cost of all roads amounted to $6,884,858, of which the federal government paid $5,071,382. In the state of Utah within that year the federal government paid 74 per cent of the construction costs, not of one highway running across the United States, or even of a federal primary highway system, but of the main interstate highways, the secondary roads, farm-to-market roads, school bus roads and rural mail delivery roads.
I fear, Mr. Speaker, that the government's formula under which it will pay only fifty per cent of the cost is not a formula that will assure the building of the trans-Canada highway even within a seven-year period; and that formula does not take into account the needs of the various provinces, the difference in construction costs, the size of population, the area and other factors which are taken into consideration in the United States formula. I rose, Mr. Speaker, mainly to point out that the minister was incorrect this morning when he said that the pattern followed in this legislation was similar to the pattern followed in the United States. I

would ask him to attempt to influence his colleagues, if he can, to bring in an adequate highway program that will meet the needs of the Canadian people, irrespective of the part of Canada in which they may reside.

speechtext:
May I refer to the point of order which has been raised? I think it would be proper to point out that the arrangement made with the Speaker while he was in the chair was that the order of speakers now being followed should be followed. In addition I might point out that since the last member of the official opposition spoke two members of the government party have spoken; therefore I do not think it can be alleged that any predominant position, even on a numerical basis, is being given to the members of the official opposition.
Speaking now to the subject matter of the bill before the house, I am certain that all the country will be glad to know that the government has now accepted the principle of federal responsibility for providing aid in the construction of a trans-Canada highway, for that acceptance is given its final form and proof in the bill which we are now considering. But at the same time I think that the country will regret the fact that this bill represents only a limited acceptance of that principle; the acceptance in this case of even the principle of providing aid to the one trans-Canada highway being limited by the features that it will be extended for only seven years and that the total amount of the aid is limited to $150 million, and for the reasons pointed out by the speaker who has just taken his seat that that amount may not be sufficient to build a first-class highway. It is also limited by the feature that no share of the cost of maintenance is to be provided by the federal government.
I also believe, Mr. Speaker, that the country will regret the fact that there has been only a limited application, or a limited acceptance of the principle which is widely accepted throughout the country, namely, that there should be federal responsibility for the joint construction and maintenance of a first-class highway system in this country. I think that is the main weakness of the bill, as is evidenced in certain particular aspects of it to which I should like to refer later.
However, as I said at the outset, I think the country will be glad that we are going as far

Trans-Canada Highway as this bill goes, if for no other reason than that it has taken us so long to get even to the point where we are beginning.
This matter first came before the parliament of Canada in a concrete way as far back as 1912, thirty-seven years ago, when the government of Sir Robert Borden introduced a bill to provide for federal aid to the provinces for the construction and maintenance of highways. It is interesting to observe that that bill passed the house. It was accepted in principle in 1912 by all parties in the house, but it was defeated in the Senate, where, at that time, there was of course a Liberal majority. For that reason the bill did not become law. Exactly the same bill was introduced in the house again in 1913. On both of these occasions the bill was introduced by the minister of transport of the day, and it had exactly the same fate. It was accepted in principle by both parties in the house. The Liberal party, which then formed the opposition, stated explicitly that, although there were some features of the bill which they did not approve of, they did agree with the principle of the provision of federal aid to the provinces for the construction and maintenance of highways. But again the bill was defeated by the overwhelming Liberal majority in the Senate at that time. The matter fell into discard during the war years from 1914 on, and it was not until 1919 under another Conservative government that the first highway aid bill finally passed both the House of Commons and the Senate and became law, providing for a limited measure of assistance by the federal government to the provinces for the purpose of constructing roads.
At that time it did not embrace merely the contemplation of one cross-country road. It was a general provision that the federal authority should aid the provinces in improving the general standard of the highway system of the country. Then, as the house knows, considerable money was spent under the provisions of the 1919 act, and further money was spent during the depression; but again the matter fell largely into disuse during the past war. In that respect it is interesting to compare our position with that of the United States, which started in 1916 with their federal aid system, and which during the war years, instead of allowing it to fall into disuse, provided for a substantial increase in the amount of federal aid to be paid out for their highways.
In 1944 they passed a statute in which they provided that for three years there should be a very substantial increase in the amount paid by the federal government in connection

with the national system of interstate highways. So we have taken from 1912 to 1949 to make a real beginning on this question of a trans-Canada road, and even now, in 1949, we are beginning well back of the point where the United States started in 1916, because in that year they laid down the basis of their federal highways system.
It is that principle upon which I submit we should be starting now, instead of on this very limited policy of providing a limited measure of aid for one trans-Canada road. There are one or two general principles I should like to suggest to the minister, because I feel that obviously he is interested in the matter and will be most anxious to see this beginning extended, and the program of which he is to be in charge expanded under a general highways system.
I would suggest first that the provision of adequate transportation in Canada is a national problem. I am sure it is scarcely necessary to develop that point beyond stating that it has been recognized as such by the initial steps taken by the federal government to provide Canada with adequate railway facilities. In those days of course highway transportation was not the chief means of transportation. However, now that it has become as important to the maintenance of our economy as has our system of railways, I feel we should extend the horizons of our thinking and take the same responsibility federally for providing adequate highway transportation as we took so many years ago to provide adequate railway transportation.
It is always to be borne in mind of course that at the present time the statutory responsibility for the construction and maintenance of highways is provincial. Therefore the second principle which it seems to me it is important to bear in mind in this connection is the necessity of working out an integrated dominion-provincial road program throughout this country. That of course is one of the chief difficulties in the evolution of any federal highways system. I think all will agree that that difficulty has been approached along sound lines in the present bill in so far as the limited scope of that bill is concerned. In it the matter of picking a route for the trans-Canada highway is to be left to the provinces, the dominion agreeing to make its contribution on a stated basis toward the construction of that route when the provinces have decided upon it.
Although a satisfactory start has been made, I should like to point out that I do not think even in that respect the bill goes as far as it should go, because the federal contribution is limited to fifty per cent of

the cost of construction, and provides nothing at all for the cost of maintenance. Surely this is an unrealistic point of view. The government is prepared to invest $150 million for the construction of a first-class trans-Canada road. Is it reasonable that when that road has been completed the government should take no interest whatever in its maintenance, no interest in the protection of its investment? I do not think that is a reasonable or businesslike attitude. In my view this does not involve any lack of confidence in the willingness or anxiety of the provinces to maintain the roads themselves.
The simple fact is that we have here the achievement of a very important measure of co-operation, where provincial and federal authorities are together going to build a trans-Canada road. Surely then the same co-operation should be extended in maintaining that joint investment, preserving the investment of the two parties. I submit it is not fair to leave it to the provinces alone to ^ bear the enormous cost of maintaining this joint investment.
This leads me to the next point I should like to discuss, which is the main weakness of the bill. That weakness all stems from the fact that the bill deals only with a specific feature of the general highways problem of the country, namely, the question of a trans-Canada road, and makes no attempt whatever to solve or even to begin to solve the general problem of providing an integrated highway system throughout the country. So that I would say the main failure of the bill is that it does not provide any basis upon which we can move forward in a systematic development of a highway system in this country.
Secondly, it fails to provide for the integration of the roads programs of the various provinces. For purposes of comparison may I here read the provisions of section 60 of the United States legislation providing for a national system of interstate highways. As has been pointed out, the first start made in the United States was a federal-aid system of highways, the basis of which has already been described. Then they gradually extended that concept of federal aid to include what is called the national system of interstate highways. Section 60 of their federal statute which deals with highways reads as follows:
There shall be designated within the continental United' States a national system of inter-state highways not exceeding forty thousand miles in total extent so located as to connect by routes, as direct as practicable, the principal metropolitan areas, cities and industrial centres, to serve the national
Trans-Canada Highway
defence, and to connect at suitable border points with routes of continental importance in the dominion of Canada and the republic of Mexico.
So that there are three features in this national system of highways: First it is to connect by as direct routes as practicable the chief metropolitan centres in the United States; secondly, it is designed to serve national defence; and, thirdly, it is to connect at suitable border points with routes in those countries bordering on the United States.
This conception of their highway system has led to that magnificent system of highways which we see and from which we benefit every time we drive in the United States; and it is that system of interstate highways which is responsible for the fact referred to by the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Argue) that the federal contribution to the total cost of highway construction is greatly in excess of the fifty per cent contemplated in our legislation.
I feel quite certain that we shall not have made any effective beginning in solving our highways problem and in meeting the requirements of an adequate road transportation system for the future development of this country until we have made a beginning along the lines of the system which has produced such magnificent results in the United States.
The third weakness which I find in the present bill stems from the same basic fault. I refer to the limitation of time during which this fund will be available, and the limitation on the total amount which will be available. Various reasons put forward this morning by the minister seem to indicate a strong possibility that the $150 million will not be sufficient to complete a first-class trans-Canada road. As he pointed out, some of the provinces may take quite a substantial proportion of the money coming to them to reimburse themselves for amounts paid out on previous road construction. Consideration must be given to the increased cost of highway construction, particularly along the rocky areas of Ontario and through the mountains of British Columbia. There are some 400 miles that would have to be traversed through the Rockies, the Selkirk, the Monashee, the Cascade and the coast ranges by any interprovincial highway in British Columbia. The increasing costs of road construction might well exhaust this fund before the objective was reached.
It may therefore be found that the funds provided are not sufficient to complete an adequate trans-Canada route and also that the time limit of seven years will not be sufficient. The government may have to

Trans-Canada Highway come back for an extension of time or for an increase in the amount, and I hope they will not hesitate to do so if it is necessary.
I assure the minister, or any other minister who may be administering this matter, that I will support such a request.
But why not avoid that likelihood? Why not lay the basis now by legislation providing for the development of an adequate system of national highways within Canada along the lines of the system in the United States? We should now lay the basis and then progressively take the necessary steps for the completion of such a system. The first step might well be the construction of a trans-Canada highway, and then other steps could be taken within the framework of the general project as provided by the legislation.
That opportunity is offered to us today and should be taken when the matter is foremost in the minds of the people. The requirements of the country indicate the necessity for such a program. I regret that a beginning has not been made in the bill before the house, but since it is better to have something than nothing at all, I shall support the bill even though I feel it is inadequate.
