First, Mr. Chairman, may I thank the Prime

Minister for affording the house this opportunity to discuss order in council P.C. 5840, which provides for the submission to the Supreme Court of Canada of a certain question in regard to the right of the federal authority to legislate by order in council or under regulations of the wartime prices and trade board under the emergency powers, to which reference has been made on a number of occasions. It was because there was such an agreement that we voted as we did a few moments ago. That arrangement having been made, apparently with the unanimous consent of the house, we endorsed it.
I should like to refer for a moment to this order in council. It is a long one, containing seven and a half pages. It consists in large part of a chronological statement setting forth the successive stages in emergency power legislation since 1945. In part it incorporates the speech made in the house on November 3, 1949, by the Minister of Finance, and it ends with the question that is submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada. That question is to be found on page 8, and reads as follows:
Are the wartime leasehold regulations ultra vires either in whole or in part and if so in what particulars or to what extent?
To begin with I submit, sir, that that question does not meet the situation at all. The succeeding paragraph reads as follows:
Therefore His Excellency the Governor General in Council, under and by virtue of the authority conferred by section 55 of the Supreme Court Act, is pleased to refer and doth hereby refer the following question to the Supreme Court of Canada for hearing and consideration.
I will not now go on to discuss what has been done nor the allowances that were given by the Minister of Finance to increase rentals on and after the 15th of December. At the moment I will consider exclusively what this order in council means, although I am fully aware of the feelings of many hundreds of thousands of the people of this country who today fear what will happen to them with the approach of the Christmas season. I do not propose for the present to deal with the hardships and the suffering that will ensue.
What I asked for the other day was an opportunity to discuss this order in council and the submission to the Supreme Court of Canada. I believe this is the first time since I have been in the house that an opportunity has been given by the government to discuss an order in council with a view to making suggestions relative to an amendment to it. I am not going into the authorities. They were all summed up recently in a case well known to the Minister of Justice-it was
Rent Control
heard in his own province-and generally to all members of the bar. I refer to the case of the Canadian Wheat Board and the Manitoba Pool Elevators, as reported in 1949, 2, Dominion Law Reports, at page 537. Summarizing that case in the words of Mr. Justice Adamson, this is what he said:
What then is the nature of the "danger," the "peril," or the "emergency" necessary to give jurisdiction to enact such legislation?
By "legislation" he means legislation by the dominion parliament, or under order in council, that results in invading property and civil rights. Then follow these significant words:
And what evidence of it is there? An emergency may be public or private. A public emergency may be local or provincial. What is necessary to justify such legislation is a national economic emergency of such dimensions as to imperil the nation, and one which would be judicially recognized in the same way as a state of war is judicially recognized.
My first point is that this order in council will be the entire reference to the Supreme Court of Canada. From beginning to end it contains not one word setting forth the facts upon which the dominion government and its counsel will rely in regard to the extent of the emergency. Having regard to the authorities, that immediately opens the door to a serious danger, in the absence of evidence to establish an emergency, by the declaration that the legislation is in fact ultra vires, and the rental orders in council will end.
I ask the government this question through the Minister of Justice. Why was this order in council worded in such general terms? Why was it not supported by evidence setting forth the necessity of such legislation or a justification for it as emergency legislation? Certainly it was not a lack of space, because the speech of the Minister of Finance on November 3 is incorporated in it. Nowhere is there anything placed before the court that sets forth the vital facts that are fundamental, namely, that there is a continuing emergency, and furthermore that that emergency will be in existence on March 31, 1950. If it is not certain that this legislation is lawful now, would it be lawful after that date? Nowhere is there any suggestion of an emergency or a continuing emergency. It must be a matter of knowledge to all hon. members in every part of the house that across this country several hundred thousand Canadians regard this situation with trepidation and fear. That there is any agreement among hon. members that there is an emergency is rather denied by the fact that the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, when speaking on March 28, 1949, as reported in the Globe and Mail

Rent Control
of March 29 and in the Montreal Gazette of the same day, to a delegation regarding the general question of housing and rental, said:
Housing was primarily a matter for the provinces except in the case of a national emergency and while the government believes there was still a great need for houses the need would not constitute an emergency.
That statement was made some four or five months ago. The declaration by a minister of the crown, as it is worded at the present time, sir, and without supporting evidence, if one were of a suspicious turn of mind, which I am not, would lead one to think that it had been deliberately worded in that way and unsupported by anything to suggest an emergency.
The next question I should like to ask is, why the indirect wording? Why not a direct wording setting out that it is being supported by evidence to justify an emergency? There is something more. When it is submitted to the supreme court how long will it be delayed before the people as a whole will know whether or not this legislation is within the power of parliament to enact by order in council? A few weeks ago we were asked in parliament to rush along the legislation making the Supreme Court of Canada the final court of appeal. The Supreme Court of Canada will not be the final court of appeal in this matter for the following reasons. The submission has already been made. I again read the second to last and operative paragraph:
Therefore His Excellency the Governor General in Council, under and1 by virtue of the authority conferred by section 55 of the Supreme Court Act-
And that is the section which provides for submissions-
-is pleased to refer and doth hereby refer the following question to the Supreme Court of Canada for hearing and consideration.
We passed the Supreme Court Act. One of the sections provides for the supreme court being the final court, and that section-the new section 54-has been passed by the Senate. Why has not royal assent been given to that act? There would be no difficulty about that. All you have to do is to bring down the deputy to His Excellency the Governor General.
Section 7 says:
Notwithstanding anything in section 3 of this act, an appeal from or in respect of a judgment pronounced in
(a)	a judicial proceeding that was commenced prior to the coming into force of this act, or
(b)	a reference made by the governor in council or by the lieutenant-governor in council of a province prior to the coming into force of this act, lies or may be brought as if that section had not been enacted.

In other words, this order in council dated November 16 provides for submission to the supreme court. The Supreme Court Act could have been assented to and brought into effect by proclamation. Then this would have been final-the first case of the Supreme Court of Canada.
That, we thought, was the idea. Indeed, one member of the press gallery in an article dated November 4, 1949-I refer to Mr. J. A. Hume-said in part:
The government plans early proclamation of legislation abolishing appeals to the judicial committee of the privy council in London, as just approved by the House of Commons and Senate.
Such action will mean that the proposed supreme court reference on the constitutionality of continuance by parliament of domestic rental controls beyond their expiry date on March 31 next would be submitted to the court here for its final judgment.
Why was not the Supreme Court Act assented to?
The result now is this, that no matter what the supreme court decides, and it will not be sitting I should think before the middle of January or early in February-because it will not be until December 1 when there will be a submission to the court for direction-the supreme court will meet and, we will suppose, hand down its answer. Perhaps it will say that it is within the legislative competence of parliament to extend rental controls. Well, then, any of the provinces can appeal, and you have uncertainty which will go on for a year or more-uncertainty, procrastination and postponement.
That, in my opinion, seems to be the reason that the order in council is drawn as it is. And one can imagine the uncertainty which will continue. Today fear stalks everywhere in our country, because of what was done on November 3. And now that fear is being accentuated by the uncertainty which will follow for a period of eight or ten months before the matter is finally decided in the privy council.
I ask the government this:	Why were
they so anxious and why did they act with such acceleration to have the Supreme Court Act amended in order to make it the final court, if the very first thing that comes up to be submitted to that court, one of the most important things to come before the court, is to be brought before it and then has to go on to the privy council in the event of appeal?
Surely it was not by inadvertence that that condition arose. I do not know of any member who was ever aware of the fact, until it came out by the veriest chance, that the

order in council had been passed on November 16. I know it was not tabled in parliament. And you will remember that when the Minister of Finance made his speech on November 3, he said this:
The order in council making the reference is being prepared and when approved will be tabled in the house.
It was approved on November 16. I believe it was last Friday that I asked a question about this order in council, and whether it would be tabled. It was tabled the next day.
Sir, is there any reason why the uncertainty and confusion should be continued, with the delay and chaos which will result? We have made the Supreme Court of Canada the final court. The government was in a terrible rush to have that effected. Would it not be possible to give to the Supreme Court of Canada, of itself, the last say? Why carry a case such as this over to the Old Country, to the privy council.
When we on this side of the house suggested that on constitutional matters appeals to the privy council should be retained the answer was, "We must be supreme in this land. Let us have our autonomy. We are an independent nation". Yet the very first thing that comes up, one of the most important matters that could be submitted to any court, leaves open the door to appeal to the privy council, with the result that this uncertainty, this chaotic condition that today exists, when one does not know for certain whether the dominion or the provinces have jurisdiction, will be continued almost indefinitely.
I suggest that another order in council should take the place of this one. If the government wants finality in this matter there should be another order in council setting out in detail the nature and the particulars of the emergency upon which the court should determine whether in fact there is an emergency. For in the last statute passed by parliament carrying on the rental controls until March 31, 1950, there is no mention of emergency in that preamble, as I read it.
Let us have royal assent to this Supreme Court Act. Then submit it to the court, and have finality, instead of having hanging over the heads of hundreds of thousands of Canadians a fear today that I doubt has been equalled at any time in the homes of the people in this dominion.
I do not know what hon. members on the government side find, but wherever I go people say to me, "We do not mind paying some increase, but allowing for the increase provided for has brought fear to us".
That being so let us know now, once and Eor all, exactly what powers are arising out of the war and in consequence of emergencies 45781-151
Rent Control
arising from the war. And, in addition, I think there might be incorporated, in addition to redrafting the question to the supreme court, which is worded in such a way that it looks as if the cart is placed before the horse -"Are the wartime leasehold regulations ultra vires either in whole or in part, and if so in what particulars and to what extent"? -a rephrasing, stating, "Are they ultra vires, and if not in what particulars?"
The wording, I think, would almost indicate a suggestion that some of them were ultra vires. Further, I think the point raised by the premier of Saskatchewan in his letter of November 16 might also find its way into that order in council, namely:
I would strongly urge your government to include in that reference a question that will settle this issue of power in yourself or the governor in council to confer legislative jurisdiction on a province by executive action designed to turn rent control over to that province.
What I have advanced in this connection has been done for one purpose, to have finality brought to this matter. Over the last two years some of the inferior courts have held that this type of legislation is beyond the powers of parliament or beyond the powers of the executive, of the governor in council under order in council. Let us bring finality to this matter which is of importance to what I imagine is the majority of people in this country. Let us not, as a result of the possibility of there being a further appeal to the privy council, leave hanging over them the uncertainty that will follow for another five, six or eight months.
Those are my suggestions. I thank the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) for the opportunity afforded to hon. members to place their views before the committee and to attempt to bring this matter into clear perspective. This is the first time that we have had a chance to discuss an order in council as is done in the British House of Commons. I think this represents additional evidence of the fact that we are returning to the democratic principles that prevailed before the war and which during the war were not followed at all times because of the necessity of concentrating power in the government during that period.

the drastic increases in rent that are permissible under the policy announced by the Minister of Finance on November 3. In common with other hon. members I have had a number of communications from people from one end of this country to the other, some in the city of Ottawa and some as far away as Vancouver and Halifax. All these communications inform me, as I am sure other hon. members have been informed, of the difficult circumstances in which they will be placed when these drastic increases are permitted to come into effect.
On November 3 the Minister of Finance evidently expected that rentals on a higher scale would go into effect and would remain in effect for a considerable time. I should like to quote from page 1434 of Hansard of November 3, 1949, where the Minister of Finance is reported to have said:
Nevertheless, it seems probable that rentals might well settle eventually at a level substantially above the present maximum levels provided in our regulations. Sooner or later the adjustment must be made, and as I have said, it is our policy to permit this adjustment to be made gradually rather than abruptly.
I do not know what is the minister's definition of "gradually", but if increases of from 18 to 22 per cent are gradual increases, then my interpretation of that word is somewhat different from that of the Minister of Finance.
With regard to the order in council, I rise mainly to suggest that the proposal made to the government in the letter of the premier of Saskatchewan should be given serious consideration and the reference which he suggests should be included in the reference to the supreme court. If we are making a reference we may as well have all doubts cleared up at the same time. I have made some inquiries and I find that not only the legal advisers of the government of Saskatchewan but other lawyers seem to believe that the doubt expressed is well founded.
The question whether we have power to confer legislative jurisdiction on one province or on any number less than all should be referred to the supreme court. I am not a lawyer and I do not profess to be able to disentangle all the legal matters in connection with a constitutional problem of this kind. I know the minister may say that there does not appear to be any doubt as to the ability of the government to do this; but if there is doubt the question should be placed before the supreme court so that it can be decided beyond any uncertainty.
No province undertaking rent control within the province should be subjected to the risk of its legislation being declared ultra vires because one or less than all the provinces

have been granted the right to pass rent control legislation by order in council and not by specific legislative action of this parliament.
The present situation is that this parliament has passed legislation which removes rent control from the provinces, a position which the premier of Quebec has been challenging ever since it was done. Rent control was placed in the hands of the federal authorities and taken out of the hands of the provinces. At the present time the legislation is applicable to all the provinces.

Except Newfoundland. I was thinking of the provinces as they existed when the legislation was passed. The legislation affected all the provinces that were provinces when it was adopted. Of course this parliament always has the right to amend its own legislation and by legislation to exclude any one province or any number of provinces from the regulations made under a statute which it has adopted.
But the question is this: Has the cabinet, the governor in council, the right to override a statute and exclude one province without having legislative authority from this parliament to make such exclusion, such distinction or such variation? I should like the minister when he replies to point out whether he considers that, under that part of our legislation giving authority for rent control, under legislation adopted by this parliament, the right to exclude one province is conferred upon the governor in council.
The point is that while the governor in council can make rental regulations inoperative in a single province, does that also give the right to the provinces to enter the field by provincial legislation when federal legislation exists claiming, rightly or wrongly, overall jurisdiction in this particular field? As I have said already, I have been advised by some legal men whose opinions I respect that there are some doubts with regard to the granting of authority by the governor in council without amending the legislation under which the governor in council proposes to act. It seems to me, then, that if there is any shadow of doubt in this connection the point should be referred to the supreme court for a ruling, or on the other hand that the federal government should ask this parliament to amend our legislation to meet the needs of one or more provinces which desire to exercise rent control provincially.
It may be possible by order in council to vacate the field of rent control on a nationwide basis and thus by implication confer jurisdiction on all the provinces at once. That,

however, seems quite different from the present proposal to confer jurisdiction on one province while jurisdiction under the statute is retained by the federal government in respect to all the other provinces. In order to avoid confusion and perhaps new difficulties or hardships the point should be referred to the supreme court for an opinion. I take it no single province wants to be placed in the position, after having made arrangements to institute rent control, after having passed the necessary legislation in that regard, of running any risk whatsoever of having that legislation upset at any time in the future.
I want to say one other thing to the minister. He has stated that in order to give any province-and Saskatchewan already has requested it-time for its legislature to pass the necessary legislation, the action of the federal government in removing or varying rent control in that province will be deferred until and including March 31 next. I suggest to the minister that having given that assurance to one province and having invited other provinces to come under the same arrangement, if they wish to do so, he should give all the provinces an opportunity to call their legislatures, and should defer the effect of the announcement he made until at least, and including, March 31 next. If this were done the provincial legislatures, which are usually called after Christmas, could meet and consider the situation and advise their governments accordingly.
This is one of the most serious steps in decontrol to be undertaken by the government since the war ended, and I do not think there is a single member of this house who does not realize that many thousands of people are going to be gravely affected. As I said, I have received a very large number of letters; in fact I do not think I have ever received more letters on any subject than on this matter of rent control. I have before me one that I am going to read in part, just to give the house an indication of the way some people fear they are going to be affected by this decontrol measure. This letter is from the father of a large family, who wishes me to withhold his name. I am under no obligation to table the document and do not intend to do so, of course. But may I comment that I frequently get letters of this description pointing out the difficulties under which Canadian men and women are working, and quite often I get the same request: "Please do not mention my name, because if it were known that I had written to you on this matter I would lose my job." That is stated in this letter. When we talk of the four freedoms, when we talk of the democracy 45781-151i

While this discussion was opened up on going into supply, Mr. Chairman, I think it must be remembered that the only matter now before us to discuss, and which can apparently be acted upon, is the reference by the government of an issue to the Supreme Court of Canada. But from the remarks that have already been made it would appear that the Prime Minister opened up this subject with the idea of affording an opportunity to discuss the issues to which this order in council relates.
The hon. member for Lake Centre has pointed out the obvious limitations in the wording of the terms of reference. In the copy of the order in council which I have before me, and which runs to eight pages, the actual terms of reference are found only at the last part of page 7 and the beginning of page 8, everything before that being a recital. The real issue that is referred to the Supreme Court of Canada is contained in less than four lines in the question: Are the

Rent Control
wartime leasehold regulations ultra vires either in whole or in part and, if so, in what particulars or to what extent?
Since we did not have an opportunity to discuss the recent changes at the time they were announced in the House of Commons, I think that on this occasion, in seeking to impress upon the government the necessity for a different type of reference, we should also point out exactly what has occurred and why the reference should be in different and wider terms. It will be recalled, particularly by those hon. members who sat in the house in the last parliament, that this subject was under discussion in March last; and on March 22, the act which has been described as the omnibus act was before the house.
It should be recalled by all the hon. members who are considering this subject at the present time that we are not discussing a rent control bill and that we are not discussing any specific piece of legislation dealing specially with rents. We are dealing with one of the continuing powers carried forward from the war under the Transitional Measures Act which was discussed by parliament last March. That bill carried forward emergency powers over rents, prices, steel, lumber, wood supplies generally and over a number of other things. That act had the effect of continuing for another year the sweeping emergency powers under which the government, by order in council, could deal with these subjects that were mentioned in that Transitional Measures Act. At that time, with other members of the house, I pointed out the difficulties that would arise unless there were introduced a bill dealing in clear and explicit terms with the problem of rent control. I would quote only briefly, to indicate the nature of the discussion which took place, from page 1767 of Hansard of March 22 last. This is from what I said at that time:
In many ways this rent control measure by government dictate is adding to the difficulties and preventing the building of satisfactory rental housing. We have urged over and over again that a rent control bill be introduced which will give tenants defined and assured legal rights and at the same time encourage the building of housing and apartments for rental purposes.
That is the parliamentary way to deal with this subject. That, Mr. Chairman, was the view that we expressed at that time. We asked that a bill, which could become the law of this parliament, be introduced, clearly defining the rights of tenants and the rights of landlords, letting each know exactly where he stood under enforceable laws. It will be recalled by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) that, along with other members of the House of Commons, I pointed out at that time that we were being asked to continue
(Mr. Drew.]
these sweeping emergency powers without any attempt being made by the government to define what the emergency actually was.
Then there is another point which the members who were sitting in the house at that time will recall. A judgment referring to one of these emergency measures had just been given by the appellate court of Manitoba. I mention that for this reason. It should be recalled that last March, when this general omnibus bill was before the house embracing not only rent control but all these other emergency measures, we pointed out that if the house were prepared to pass legislation then tenants and landlords should sit down with a law which clearly stated their rights, and they would know where they were for a definite period; but that the continuing of this list of indefinite emergency powers would only create the very type of confusion that has arisen.
In spite of the arguments we put forward at that time this parliament was asked by the government to declare that there was an emergency, because it was necessary to declare that in effect if this sweeping bill was to be passed, and that decision was made.
It seems a strange thing at this time, Mr. Chairman, to come forward and say: We are going to ask the Supreme Court of Canada if there is or is not an emergency of the nature that would support the rental measures, but we are not going to say anything at all about the rest of the emergency measures that are carried forward in the same legislation. If there is an emergency that supports the continuance of these measures, then that same emergency must support the continuance of the other measures, and the same is true in reverse.

Mr. Chairman, before my colleague the Minister of Justice says a word about the legal question involved concerning the order in council, perhaps I might be permitted to say a word in connection with policy in reply to some questions raised by the leader of the opposition, and the leader of the C.C.F.
First I should like to put the record straight as to the chronological order in which the government has attacked this question of decontrol of rentals. On October 23 of last year- that is, October 23, 1948-I wrote a letter in substantially the same terms to all the provincial premiers. I have not that letter at hand, because I did not think it would be necessary to quote it tonight; however, in the 45781-152
Rent Control
letters which I wrote to the premiers recently in connection with the new announcement I quoted from that earlier letter.
On October 23, 1948, as I say, I wrote to the provincial premiers pointing out that the dominion government had entered the field of rental control along with price control, wage control and other controls as a wartime measure, as part of an over-all control system; it being considered that it had no constitutional power to remain in the field indefinitely and was under obligation to proceed to the decontrol of rentals as well as of other controls as rapidly as circumstances would permit. To that end it indicated to the provincial governments that they should give consideration at that time to entering the field if in their judgment they felt it was desirable to do so. Here is what 1 said to the provincial premiers, and I quote from my letter to the premier of Quebec of October 23, 1948:
At the same time the federal government is prepared to vacate the field at any time after March 31, 1949, to any province which may decide to undertake rent control. Normally rent control would come under provincial jurisdiction and is peculiarly suitable for provincial or local administration because of the immovable nature of real property. The federal government is anxious not to stand in the way of any province which believes that rent control can be better undertaken and administered locally.
This announcement of policy is being made at this time so that any provincial government which wishes to do so will have sufficient time to prepare legislation for presentation to its legislature before March 31, 1949.
For reasons which no doubt seemed wise to them no provincial government came forward and suggested that it would introduce rental control legislation. The dominion government in February or March of this year, feeling that a condition still existed which justified it in going before parliament and asking for an extension of its power to continue to exercise rent control, discharged that responsibility and the bill ,to which my hon. friend referred was passed. In the letters which were tabled the other day, that offer was repeated. I should say that in the meantime the new province of Newfoundland had come into confederation. Newfoundland had had a rental control system in force before that time and it has continued to exercise its own control over rentals.
Then as to the matter of policy. As I said a moment ago, the federal government feels that it has no constitutional right to continue indefinitely in this field, that it has no right other than to continue to decontrol as rapidly as circumstances will permit. As hon. members know, more than four years after the end of the war we were out of all the major controls; we are out of price control, we are

Rent Control
out of wage control, and we are out of most of the other controls. In fact I think steel control is pretty well the only one left.
If anyone could give me a good reason why we should continue to exercise control over one relatively small group in the community, the owners of housing accommodation, I wish he would give it to me because no one has given it to me yet. Everyone has said that there is going to be hardship involved if the apparently large number of tenants have to pay higher rents, but that is no answer to me as to why four years after the war the central government in Ottawa should assert the right to continue to tell one small group in the community what they shall receive when they do not attempt to control anybody else.
No one on the other side has attempted to answer that. Hon. members on the other side have made a lot of demagogic appeals about the hardship that is going to be involved. They have read from letters from people who in some cases are going to find it hard to meet these increased rentals. But that is no way of solving the problem. It is not solved by the dominion government continuing to occupy a field in which its powers are definitely limited.
All I am saying on the grounds of policy is that the provincial governments of this country had an opportunity last fall to adopt rental control legislation if they wished to do so. Up to the present time only one province has indicated its intention to do so. As far as I am concerned, and as the Prime Minister suggested the other day, any province which wishes to do so may come forward and say that it intends to do so, and it will get the same treatment as the province of Saskatchewan.
I am not going to deal with the legal matters raised by the hon. member for Lake Centre, because my colleague the Minister of Justice will do that; but it seemed to me it might be appropriate at this stage for me to say a few words in addition to what I said a week or ten days ago as to the reasons which prompted the government in taking this action.

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY WITH RESPECT TO MARKETING
speechtext:
I wonder if I might be permitted to deal with some of the points raised by speakers on the opposition side of the house. The leader of the opposition made the statement that either the government is in doubt about its power or it is not. I suggest that by no more complicated a device than reading the order in council which is the subject of this discussion he could have set at rest any doubts he might have had on that score.
As my colleague the Minister of Finance has indicated, government policy with respect to this rental matter is that of orderly decontrol; but inasmuch as our jurisdiction in this field, which ordinarily would be with the provinces, is based upon the continuation of an emergency arising out of war, it is quite obvious that with the lapse of time after the end of hostilities the factual basis for the exercise of federal jurisdiction becomes less and less. Therefore when we address ourselves to the question whether it is possible to complete a program of decontrol by March 31, 1950, we reach the opinion, stated in this

Rent Control
order in council, that we cannot complete that program by that time. Then in spite of the fact that we have no doubt ourselves as to our legal position, since we shall be taking a step which will extend these emergency measures for a year from March, 1950, it would seem that not out of an abundance of caution but out of a reasonable amount of caution we should submit this question to the court upon a reference. In case there should be any doubt as to our own view I would refer my hon. friend the leader of the opposition to page 5 of the order in council, of which I think he has a copy, where the speech of my colleague the Minister of Finance is quoted in these words:
May I say at this point that the advice which the government receives from its law officers is that the existing federal regulations with respect to rent control are valid.
Then further down:
As I have said, the law officers of the crown are of opinion that the rentals regulations are valid. They are also of opinion that both the law and the facts support the view that it lies within the authority of parliament to extend these regulations for a further period. Counsel will be instructed by the Attorney General of Canada to press this view before the court.
So there is no doubt as to the view of the government. We think we have the power and that these regulations are valid. It is only of a very proper caution that-some four years after the end of the war, as my colleague has pointed out-we think that before we extend these powers for a further period of one year we should have them passed upon by the court.
The leader of the opposition asked why, in the order in council establishing a reference, we should be bothering with the wartime leasehold regulations. He said this matter arose under the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, and asked why we did not refer the act itself to the court. I must apologize to the legal members of the house, because these are elementary principles of law, but I suggest that the first thing the dominion parliament requires in order to exercise jurisdiction in a field that normally belongs to the provinces is some type of wartime emergency such as we have here, a set of facts upon which to base its jurisdiction. Once it has those it passes a law, which in this case, as my hon. friend correctly says, is the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act. Then, pursuant to that statute, the governor general in council passes certain regulations.
When we submit to the court the question whether these regulations are ultra vires, that submission embraces first of all the question whether the governor general, in passing the regulations, has acted within the ambit

of the powers given by the statute, and secondly whether the statute itself is within the powers of parliament. So it is quite idle to draw the distinction my hon. friend the leader of the opposition has attempted to draw, between the regulations upon the one hand and the act upon the other in a reference such as this. The two of them are, for the purpose of a reference of this sort, inseparable.

Not if the court's findings are based upon the view that the governor in council, in passing the leasehold regulations, has exceeded the authority granted by the act.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said that there might be some insufficiency or difficulty in the act authorizing the governor in council to implement this arrangement which is under negotiation between the federal government and the Saskatchewan government. If that be so I should think that, inasmuch as this arrangement will come into effect some time later, it would be a simple matter, since we must apply within sixty days after the meeting of the

1950 session of parliament for an extension of this authority, to take the necessary statutory authority at that time.
From the government's standpoint, Mr. Chairman, and particularly from the standpoint of the Department of Justice, this discussion has been worth while. We have had the benefit of the views of such eminent lawyers as the hon. member for Lake Centre, and of some of the legally minded laymen of the house, in suggesting the various considerations that we might take under advisement in connection with this reference. I should like to congratulate my hon. friends upon the very useful statements they have made in this debate. We are greatly indebted to them for those suggestions, in spite of the fact that I have a sufficient feeling of confidence in the deputy minister and his advisers that I believe it probable they have considered each of these alternatives now suggested and have rejected them in favour of the course which is set out in P.C. 5840. The fact that they may have done so does not in any way lessen our gratitude for those suggestions that have been made.
In dealing with those suggestions, I hope my hon. friends opposite did not cherish the illusion that I was going to come here to debate these legal points with them, because I am in a much different position, as minister, than they are as members of the opposition. If they discuss, in terms of legal generalities, a number of abstract principles of constitutional law they are not discussing-at least I am charitable enough to assume they are not-a matter that is sub judice, which is contrary to the rules of this house. But if I considered their suggestions as alternatives to the course we have adopted in this order in council, I would be under the necessity of outlining the case that we are going to present to the Supreme Court of Canada. In that event I should certainly be offending the rules of this house which declare that it is improper for a member to discuss a matter which is under consideration by the courts.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Winters for the second reading of Bill No. 194, to encourage and to assist in the construction of a trans-Canada highway.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I will not keep the house long, Mr. Speaker, because there has been a considerable amount of debate on this bill in connection with the all-Canada highway. I think it has been fairly well covered. From this corner of the house in the Social Credit group the leader, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), spoke on the matter when it was in the resolution stage. The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), who has made a special study of this matter, has given two major speeches on it. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) has spoken on it. There is therefore not a great deal left for me to say, but I think I should put in my little ten cents' worth.
I know that it is not a particularly popular course to follow in this house for one to proceed now to make any recommendations as to the route the highway should take. Nevertheless, I am going to run the chance of becoming unpopular and suggest that, with regard to Alberta and British Columbia, the route should be through the southern

portion of Alberta, through Lethbridge, through the Crowsnest pass and in that direction. The reason I am saying this is that I believe special factors enter into the picture. A road built along that route would make beautiful and convenient connections with the various highways in the United States. This would facilitate tourist traffic coming into Canada and going up to the beauty spots of the rockies. Another matter to be considered with respect to the route which the highway should follow is the population: How many people will the highway serve? While I have not all the exact statistics on this matter, I believe that the route going through the Crowsnest pass and the southern part of British Columbia would serve a larger population compared with other routes through Alberta and British Columbia.
Another matter is the length of the road in mileage. I believe that that route is perhaps one of the shortest ones. I agree, however, with the hon. member for Lethbridge and others who have spoken that we must think not merely in terms of one coast-to-coast highway but of a real system of federal highways in Canada so that no matter what route the main highway may take, all other routes will be served.
There is one matter that I should like to bring to the attention of the house, and it has been mentioned before. I cannot quite understand why the government are proposing a seven-year period for the construction of this highway. I am not an engineer and I am therefore not going to attempt to argue all the details of construction that may be necessary; but for the life of me I cannot see why it should take seven years to build that highway. I recognize that if one contractor or one construction company were to begin at Halifax and eventually end in Vancouver, it might take even seventy years. I do not believe that is the way the highway will be built. I believe that many construction companies will do the work according to the contracts awarded them for the building of this highway. I cannot see why it should take seven years. I just wonder whether the government may think that there is a depression lurking somewhere around the corner, and that in order to absorb the shock of unemployment they will propose a seven-year period and use the all-Canada highway for that purpose. That is the only answer that I can think of. If that is going to be so then I say the government is not tackling the highway problem at all. They are simply making future plans to assist in a possible situation which they think might develop.

In previous speeches that have been made I noticed that the minister has been congratulated a good deal for introducing this measure and deciding to build this coast to coast highway. I do not want to be unkind, but I am not going to congratulate the minister at all, because I do not believe that he is the one particularly responsible for initiating the move. I am going to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that some of us have been advocating an all-Canada highway for a good many years. I suppose hon. members stood up in this house before many of us ever came here and recommended an all-Canada highway. In the fourteen years that we have been here we have advocated it over and over again. I am particularly reminded of the fact that some months previous to the last election the leader of the Progressive Conservatives-perhaps he was a little premature-made the announcement-if it was not he then it came from the Progressive Conservative convention; I am not certain of the origin of it, but I know it came from Progressive Conservative quarters -that if they were elected they would pursue a policy that would give Canada an allCanadian highway. He had not mentioned it very long before the government arose and stole his thunder. They announced that they were going to build this highway, placing emphasis upon the fact that they were in office and were in a better position to build a highway than some party that was not yet in office. They put the matter in the hands of the then minister of mines and resources, a greatly honoured gentleman who now sits in another place. Pressure began to be placed upon him for the highway to take a certain route which would cover his constituency. Perhaps considering that the highway might not go through his constituency they recognized that they were in a bit of a jam. What did they do? They moved the all-Canada highway from the jurisdiction of the Minister of Mines and Resources and put it into the hands of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, who did not live in northern Alberta, but lived away down here in the maritime provinces. Therefore that little political fence was hurdled.
Then came the election. The Liberals had stolen the thunder of the Progressive Conservatives. They were elected, and now they have to bring down a bill, and everyone in the house rises and congratulates the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply on his vision and his courage in introducing this bill. So much for that.
I want to know why it is going to take seven years to build this highway? The only thing I can suggest is that they expect a period of unemployment. They will get their picks and shovels out. They will bring in all
Trans-Canada Highway the unemployed and say: "Here you are. Here are your picks and shovels. The engineers have gone out. Now we shall give you a job to do."
I might say that while the leader of the Progressive Conservatives did advocate this highway previous to the election, there is one point that we have lost sight of, namely, that the Conservative party, under the late Mr. Bennett, when he was prime minister of Canada, was one jump ahead of them all. He started an all-Canada highway, but-there is a "but" in there-he started it not because Canada needed an all-Canada highway. That was not the purpose of the highway. There was a depression and vast unemployment. The purpose of the highway was to put the unemployed people to work. So he gave them picks and shovels and put them out in the northern part of Ontario to dig their way through the bush, at, I am told, $5 a week. A portion of that highway was referred to this morning by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston).
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) said that he had travelled all over it. He did not travel all over it because he did not know it was there. I will tell you why he did not know it was there. After about fifteen or twenty years the trees have grown up in the middle of the highway. There are trees in the middle of that highway with trunks almost as large as the circumference of my body, and that is getting larger and larger at about the same rate as the trees get larger and larger.
Mr. Bennett started to build that road and every time it came to a river it stopped. Of course the unemployed could not build bridges very well. It took expensive engineering skill to do that, so the highway stopped. If you wish to go over the highway you will need a puddle jumper to jump over the rivers and streams where the highway stopped. When you are going along in a train you can see the highway more or less close or farther away as the case may be with trees growing up in the middle of it. I am wondering whether the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) is going to follow that same highway. Part of the work may be done, but I am afraid that he will have to rebuild it. If he follows it he will at least have to cut all the timber off it and he will have to build bridges and so forth. I shall leave that for him to do. The fact of the matter is that governments have monkeyed around with this all-Canada highway for many many years and still we have not one.
Now we are about to have one, and it is going to be seven years before the ultimate objective will be realized. For the life of

Trans-Canada Highway me, with modern road-building machinery such as we have in Canada, I do not see why it should take more than three or at the outside four years to build that highway. Let us get started at it and have the highway built as soon as possible.
A good deal of it is already built by the provinces. Whether the parts now built will meet the specifications the minister has in mind, I cannot say. I will say this, however, that there are portions built which I am sure are better than the specifications the minister has. We have some mighty fine roads in Alberta-and I might as well put in a plug for my native province. I will say, too, that some portions of roads I have seen in British Columbia will match any to be found on the North American continent-perhaps not in width, but certainly in the travelling conditions offered by those highways. While there are not many of them, some which have been built recently would be a matter of pride to any country.
I travelled a small portion built in the last couple of years just this side of Cranbrook in British Columbia, and I am going to say that if the minister wishes to travel on a beautiful piece of road he should try that piece. While it is only about fifteen miles in length, he will think he is travelling on a piece of glass. The engineering skill has been marvellous.
I believe that is all I have to say. When the minister builds this highway I wonder if he will tell us just why he considers it will take seven years. For the life of me I cannot see why it should.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to make only a few brief observations on the bill, most of which are occasioned by what was said by a previous speaker.
I rise to support the principle of the bill, and to say that I listened with great interest to the statement of the minister when he introduced it. I believe it is safe to say that finally the government has reacted to some extent satisfactorily to public demand across Canada for the commencement of this work.
I have one or two criticisms of the bill, while supporting it in principle. My first criticism is that I am sorry the bill does not provide for a trans-Canada highway system. While that may not be possible immediately,

I am of the opinion that in starting this most important legislation for the Canadian people we should have had in the bill a provision for a trans-Canada highway system. I find that is what organizations throughout British Columbia had been asking for. As I said before, while it may not be possible to do these things immediately, we should have made provision for them and have indicated to the people of Canada that the government intended over a period of years to develop a trans-Canada highway system.
I think the necessity for such a system is obvious when we listen to the discussion concerning the various routes suggested across Canada. It is only natural that a province will favour a district in which it is interested. We in British Columbia are particularly interested in three routes, namely the Crows-nest pass, the Big Bend or central route, and the Yellowhead pass route. No matter which one is built first, there can be no question that the three routes will have to be built eventually, if British Columbia is to be served satisfactorily so far as a trans-Canada highway system is concerned.
I heartily support the Crowsnest route and I believe that it is the most suitable and should be built first. I shall not discuss that question now in detail, because the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) spoke at some length in support of it, and there is no need to repeat his argument. I do think however that in dealing with this matter we should approach it not from the standpoint of this or that route, but rather as Canadians hoping to see at least one trans-Canada highway from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
Then, while we are seriously concerned with the percentage the federal government will pay, we must realize that finally, while the federal government pays a certain percentage and the provincial government a certain percentage, the whole of the expense comes out of the taxpayers' pockets. Therefore as our first objective we should have a trans-Canada system.
When approaching a matter of this kind I am inclined to set limited objectives, something reasonably possible within the reasonably near future. On that point I disagree with the bill, because I believe provision should have been made for a trans-Canada highway system, although only one route is to be proceeded with at the present time. When we have a trans-Canada highway system complete and serving all the areas of Canada satisfactorily, it will be time then for the federal and provincial governments to get together to arrange for the building of satisfactory farm roads.

I am pleased to see in the bill a provision for a fifty per cent payment to the provinces in respect of money already expended for the building of portions of highways which will become part of the trans-Canada highway route. I believe this will tend to equalize the great differences in the cost of building highways in the various portions of Canada.
I may have misunderstood the minister, but I would suggest that the fifty per cent returnable to any province on account of money formerly expended for the building of a portion of the trans-Canada highway should be earmarked for future highway construction in that province. I am of the opinion that in view of the large amount of money spent by the provinces which will be included in the trans-Canada highway when its final location is decided upon, and in view of the large amount of money to be repaid to the provinces on that basis alone, the $150 million will soon be found insufficient to complete the work. If we develop a trans-Canada highway system probably it would have been more sound to have made provision whereby the federal government would have paid seventy-five per cent and the provincial governments twenty-five per cent, as is done in respect of other legislation in which the federal and provincial governments are interested.
I was glad to hear the minister's statement with regard to standards and from what I was able to hear I think satisfactory standards have been established at this time. Naturally in the mountains those standards will be different than in the prairie provinces and other parts of Canada where road building is easier and traffic heavier. It must be remembered that when you come to construct a highway in mountainous country with its rock cliffs and things like that you multiply the cost of construction manyfold by every additional five feet in width. We must have different standards, not only with regard to width but with regard to grades and curvatures.
There is one thing I should like to draw to the attention of the minister, a thing which has been overlooked in the past by provincial governments when undertaking highway construction. You see examples all across the country where narrow bridges are used to connect two wider sections of highway. It is most necessary that all bridges be built to standard so that they will serve for many years to come.
I think one member stated that a one hundred foot allowance was too wide for certain portions of the maritime provinces. If we are going to have a satisfactory highway in the mountainous regions in many cases
Trans-Canada Highway the allowance will have to be five hundred feet because of the angle of the slopes and so on.
One other hon. member referred to the necessity of connecting up the various cities in Canada, but I am not in agreement with that. If we are going to build a satisfactory trans-Canada highway that will provide a through route it must be built in the best location possible whether or not it by-passes any particular city, village or town. It will be quite easy for any city, town or village to construct connecting links.
These are all the observations I want to make at this time except to express again my regret that this bill, which is the commencement of something that will eventually develop into a very large project in a few years, does not provide for a trans-Canada highway system.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
